1.text:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., and under conditional unconfoundedness
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$, $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$
a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. With a binary $D$
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The $1,D$ projection is the ATE.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]+E[\tau(X)|D=1]$.
The selection term is unrestricted.  With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and
$m_{0}(x)$ increasing in $X$ it can dominate $E[\tau(X)|D=1]$, e.g.
$X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$, $m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$,
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.  The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ is not sign identified.

Case 3. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$ and the population linear projection on $1,D,X$
is used. Let $\tilde D$ be the linear residual of $D$ after projection on
$1,X$, $\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$. Then
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X),\tilde D\big)+
Cov\big(p(X)\tau(X),\tilde D\big)$.
The first term $>0$.  $\tilde D$ is the linear residual of $D$ w.r.t.
$X$, i.e. $E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)$.  With no linearity
restriction on $m_{0}(\cdot)$ or $p(\cdot)$ the term
$Cov(m_{0}(X),\tilde D)$ is unrestricted.  It can be made arbitrarily
negative.

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$.  Then
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$, $Cov(D,X)=0$, and the linear
projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$ has $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ for
$M$ large so $\beta_{3}<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s.

The sign preserving quantity is the non-parametric partial out
$Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$, i.e. a saturated control for $X$.
Under the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’ the
strictly linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$ does not preserve the sign.

Hence with the stated non-parametric conditions the only robust sign
guarantee for the population OLS $D$ coefficient is unconditional
randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

6.text:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$ with $\tau_i=Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)>0$ a.s. and under
conditional unconfoundedness

$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

* Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))$. For a binary $D$

$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0,$

the ATE. Unconditional randomisation is sign identified.

* Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
=E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]+E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is free.
With $p(x)=P(D=1\mid X=x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(x)$ increasing in
$X$, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=100,
\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The marginal $1+D$
projection is not sign identified.

* Case 3. The population regression is the linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$.
Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Then $\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]+Cov\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),
E[\tilde D\mid X]\big)$.
The first term is $>0$, but $E[\tilde D\mid X]=p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)$ is the
non-linear part of the propensity. $Cov(m_{0}(X),\tilde D)$ is
unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions. With
$X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equal prob., $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)=0,m_{0}(1)=M\gg0,\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$
for every $x$ but $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ and the linear projection
$Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_{3}<0$. The same
construction works with $m_{0}(X)=X^{2},p(X)=X^{2}$ giving
$\beta_{3}=\tau-1<0$ for $0<\tau<1$.

The strictly positive weighted average 
$E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$ is the coefficient on the
non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$. The stated $1+D+X$ linear
projection uses the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Without a
linearity restriction on $E[Y\mid X]$ and $E[D\mid X]$ the linear
misspecification bias $Cov(m_{0}(X),\tilde D)$ can dominate and flip the
sign.

Hence under the literal linear OLS and no further parametric
assumption the only robustly sign-forced population $D$ coefficient is
unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

If $X$ is understood to be controlled for non-parametrically, $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ and the conventional textbook statement is Cases 1 and 3, i.e. E.

11.text:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and with conditional unconfoundedness
$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$ and $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$
a.s. $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. For a binary $D$
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The bivariate projection is the ATE.

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
 =E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted.
With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(x)$ increasing in $X$,
e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$,
$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$.  Sign not guaranteed.

Case 3. The population linear projection on $1,D,X$ is
$\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,D^{\perp})/Var(D^{\perp})$ with $D^{\perp}=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$.
$E[D^{\perp}\mid X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$ is the non-linear part of the
propensity. With $Y=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)+\eta$,
$Cov(Y,D^{\perp})=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X),E[D^{\perp}\mid X]\big)
+...$.
The first term $>0$ but $Cov\big(m_{0}(X),E[D^{\perp}\mid X]\big)$ is unrestricted
under the stated non-parametric conditions.  The linear residual $D^{\perp}$
is not $D-E[D\mid X]$ unless $p(X)$ is linear in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ is linear
in $X$.

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ with equal mass, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)=0,m_{0}(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$.
Then $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$ and
$Cov(D,X)=0$, yet $Cov(Y,D)<0$ for $M$ large and the linear projection of $Y$
on $1,D,X$ has $\beta_{3}<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(d)\mid X$.

Hence the non-parametric within-$X$ contrast $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]
=\tau(X)>0$ is positive, but the linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$ does not
inherit the sign without a linearity restriction on $E[Y\mid X]$ and $E[D\mid X]$.
With no parametric assumptions beyond those given, the only sign
guarantee for the population OLS $D$ coefficient is unconditional
randomisation.

A. Only Case 1.

4.text:
With potential outcomes $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i=Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)>0$ a.s.
and conditional unconfoundedness

$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,  
$m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s.,  
$p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.

* Case 1. $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$.
For a binary $D$
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The $1+D$ linear projection is the ATE and is strictly positive.

* Case 2. $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
 =E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted.
With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(x)$ increasing in $X$ it can
dominate $E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]$.  e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$.
The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ projection is not sign identified.

* Case 3. $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ and the population linear projection
$Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$ is used. Let $D_{p}={\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$,
$D_{r}=D-D_{p}$. Then

$\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,D_{r})/Var(D_{r})$.

Writing $Y=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)+\eta$,

$Cov(Y,D_{r})=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X),p(X)-D_{p}(X)\big)$

up to $\tau$ terms.  $E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$ but
$E[D_{r}\mid X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\neq0$ whenever $p(X)$ is
non-linear in $X$.  Hence $Cov(m_{0}(X),D_{r})$ is the covariance of the
non-linear part of $m_{0}$ with the non-linear part of $p$ and is
unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions.

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equal prob., $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)=0,m_{0}(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$, gives
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$ but
$Cov(Y,D)<0$ for $M$ large and the linear projection on $1,D,X$ has
$\beta_{3}<0$.  The same sign reversal occurs with $m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$,
$p(x)=x^{2}$.

The non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$ would give
$\beta^{np}=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$, i.e. the textbook
within-$X$ sign preservation.  With the literal linear regression
$Y\sim1+D+X$ and no parametric restriction on $m_{0}(\cdot)$ or
$p(\cdot)$ the misspecification bias $Cov(m_{0}(X),D_{r})$ can dominate
the positive $E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]$ term.

Hence under the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’
the strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced only by
unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

8.text:
With $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau=Y(1)-Y(0)>0$ a.s. and conditional unconfoundedness

$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,  $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s.,  $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

*Case 1* $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. For a binary $D$
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The bivariate linear projection is the ATE. Sign is forced.

*Case 2* $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
      =E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
$E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is
unrestricted. With $p(x)=P(D=1\mid X=x)$ decreasing in $X$ and
$m_{0}(x)$ increasing in $X$ the selection term can dominate the
positive treatment term, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_{0}(L)=0,
m_{0}(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$.
The $1+D$ OLS is not sign identified.

*Case 3* $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ and $Y$ is the linear projection on
$1,D,X$.  Put $D^{\perp}=D-{\rm Proj}_{lin}(D\mid1,X)$. Then
$\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,D^{\perp})/Var(D^{\perp})$.
$Cov(Y,D-E[D\mid X])=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$, so the non–parametric
residual $D-E[D\mid X]$ is sign preserving.  The linear residual
$D^{\perp}$ differs from $D-E[D\mid X]$ whenever $E[D\mid X]=p(X)$ is
non-linear in $X$.  Write

$Cov(Y,D^{\perp})=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X),E[D^{\perp}\mid X]\big)
+{\rm remainder}$,

$E[D^{\perp}\mid X]=p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)$ is the non-linear part of the
propensity.  $Cov\big(m_{0}(X),E[D^{\perp}\mid X]\big)$ is unrestricted
under the stated non-parametric conditions.

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)=0,m_{0}(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$.  Then
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$ and $D\perp Y(d)\mid X$,
yet $Cov(Y,D)<0$ for $M$ large and the population least squares
solution of $Y=\alpha+\beta_{D}D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_{D}<0$.
The same holds with $m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$ and $p(x)=x^{2}$, giving
$\beta_{3}=\tau-1<0$ for $0<\tau<1$.

Hence the within-$X$ mean difference $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]
=\tau(X)>0$ is positive, i.e. the non-parametric control for $X$ is sign
preserving, but the linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$ is not without an
extra linearity restriction on $E[Y\mid X]$ and $E[D\mid X]$.

With no parametric assumptions beyond those stated the only population
OLS coefficient that is necessarily $>0$ is the unconditionally
randomised difference in means.

A. Only Case 1

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Case 1 is sign identified and Case 2 is not, and Case 3 is sign identified.

With potential outcomes $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., the conditional unconfoundedness assumption is
$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_0(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ with $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$ and $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. Then for binary $D$
$\beta_1=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The $1+D$ projection is the ATE.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D$ is generally correlated with $X$.
$\beta_2=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$.
The first term is $>0$ but the selection term $E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted. With pre-income $X$ increasing in $Y(0)$ and $P(D=1\mid X)=p(X)$ decreasing in $X$, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_0(L)=0,m_0(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$, we get $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ regression can be negative even though $\tau_i>0$ a.s.

Case 3. Put $X$ in the regression. Let $\tilde D$ be the part of $D$ orthogonal to the linear span of $1,X$, so by Frisch-Waugh
$\beta_3=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$.
Conditional on $X$, $D\perp Y(0)\mid X$, so
$E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y\mid X]=E[(D-E[D\mid X])^2\mid X]\,\tau(X)$.
Hence
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Cov(Y,D\mid X)]=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$,
and $Var(\tilde D)=E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$.
Thus
$\beta_3=\dfrac{E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]}{E[Var(D\mid X)]}=E_w[\tau(X)]>0$,
a $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ effects $\tau(X)=E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]>0$.

In words, once $X$ is partialled out the residual variation in $D$ is mean independent of any function of $X$. $E[Y(0)\mid X]=m_0(X)$ is fully absorbed by the $X$ regressor, so the only covariance that remains between the $X$-residualised $D$ and $Y$ is the within-$X$ gain $Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)>0$. Controlling for pre-treatment income removes the $X$-selection that reverses Case 2, and the partial association of $D$ with $Y$ inherits the sign of the conditional treatment effect.

So the $D$ coefficient is necessarily $>0$ under unconditional randomisation, Case 1, and under conditional randomisation once $X$ is controlled for, Case 3, whereas the uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2, is not sign protected. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With $Y = Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., conditional unconfoundedness is
$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]\equiv m_0(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ with $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. For a binary $D$
$\beta_1=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation is the ATE, sign forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D$ is in general correlated with $X$.
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$.
The second term is $X$ selection on the baseline. With $p(x)=P(D=1\mid X=x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(x)$ increasing in $X$, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9$, $p(H)=0.1$, $m_0(L)=0$, $m_0(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$,
$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ regression is not sign identified, the classic Simpson reversal from targeting the jobs programme to low pre-income workers.

Case 3. Add $X$ to the regression. Let $D^{\perp}$ be the part of $D$ orthogonal to $1,X$. By Frisch-Waugh
$\beta_3={\rm Cov}(Y,D^{\perp})/{\rm Var}(D^{\perp})$.
Conditional on $X$,
$E[Y D\mid X]=E[Y\mid X]E[D\mid X]+{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)$
because $E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y(0)\mid X]=0$ under $D\perp Y(0)\mid X$.
Hence
${\rm Cov}(Y,D^{\perp})=E\!\left[{\rm Cov}(Y,D\mid X)\right]
=E\!\left[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)\right]>0$
and
${\rm Var}(D^{\perp})=E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]>0$.
So
$\beta_3=\dfrac{E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)]}{E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]}
=E_w[\tau(X)]>0$,
a ${\rm Var}(D\mid X)$-weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ effects $\tau(X)=E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]>0$.

In words, once pre-treatment income is partialled out the residual variation in $D$ is mean independent of $Y(0)$ given $X$. Within every $X$ stratum $D$ is as good as random and $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$. Controlling for $X$ removes the baseline selection that drives Case 2 and the partial association of $D$ with $Y$ inherits the sign of the within-$X$ treatment gain.

Therefore the population $D$ coefficient is necessarily $>0$ under unconditional randomisation, Case 1, and under conditional randomisation once $X$ is controlled for, Case 3, whereas the uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2, can be negative.

That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

12.text:
The population coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.  
Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., and under the stated
conditional unconfoundedness

$E[Y\mid X,D]=\mu_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$ ,  $\mu_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s.  Put $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$.

* Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))$. With a binary $D$

$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$,

the difference in means, i.e. the ATE. The sign is forced.

* Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
\[
\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
      =E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=0]+E[\tau(X)\mid D=1].
\]
$E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but the selection term
$E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is free. With $p(x)$
decreasing in $x$ and $\mu_{0}(x)$ increasing in $x$ it can dominate
the treatment term.  E.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9$, $p(H)=0.1$,
$\mu_{0}(L)=0$, $\mu_{0}(H)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$, gives
$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<M\cdot 0.1+... <E[Y\mid D=0]$. The $1+D$ projection
is not sign identified.

* Case 3.  Let $P_{1,X}$ be linear projection on $1,X$ and
$\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$, $\tilde Y=Y-P_{1,X}Y$. Then
$\beta_{3}=E[\tilde D Y]/E[\tilde D^{2}]$. Now
\[
E[\tilde D Y]=E[\tilde D^{2}\tau(X)]+E[\tilde D\mu_{0}(X)],
\]
$E[\tilde D^{2}\tau(X)]>0$ but
$E[\tilde D\mu_{0}(X)]=E[\tilde D(\mu_{0}(X)-P_{1,X}\mu_{0}(X))]$
is unrestricted. $\tilde D$ is the linear residual of $D$ w.r.t. $X$,
not the non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$. If $p(X)$ is non-linear
in $X$ then $E[\tilde D\mid X]=p(X)-P_{1,X}p(X)\neq0$ and it can be
made negatively correlated with the non-linear part of $\mu_{0}(X)$.

For instance $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equally likely,
$p(0)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $\mu_{0}(0)=\mu_{0}(2)=0$, $\mu_{0}(1)=M\gg0$,
$\tau\equiv1$. Then $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$,
${\rm Cov}(D,X)=0$, but the population linear projection
$Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$ has
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)<0$ for $M$ large, i.e. $\beta_{3}<0$, although
$Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

Hence $E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]>0$ for the
non-parametric partial-out $D-E[D\mid X]$, which is the textbook
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.  With the literal linear
projection $Y\sim1+D+X$ and no linearity restriction on
$\mu_{0}(X)$ and on $p(X)$ the linear misspecification bias
${\rm Cov}\big(\mu_{0}(X),D-P_{1,X}D\big)$ can be made arbitrarily
negative and flip the sign.

Under the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’ the
only sign guarantee for the population OLS $D$ coefficient is
unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

If $X$ is understood as being controlled for non-parametrically the
textbook statement is that the within-$X$ mean difference is positive,
so Cases 1 and the non-parametric version of Case 3 are sign
preserving.

15.text:
With $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and conditional unconfoundedness

$$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]=\mu_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X),\qquad
\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0\;{\rm a.s.}$$

and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$.  For binary $D$

$$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0,$$

the usual difference in means, i.e. the ATE. Unconditional randomisation
is sign identified.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general.

$$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
       =E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=0]+E[\tau(X)\mid D=1].$$

$E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but the selection term is unrestricted. With
$p(x)=P(D=1\mid X=x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $\mu_{0}(x)$ increasing in $X$
the bias can dominate the treatment term.  E.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$,
$p(L)=0.9$, $p(H)=0.1$, $\mu_{0}(L)=0$, $\mu_{0}(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$,

$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$

although $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. The $Y\sim1+D$ population OLS is not sign
identified.

Case 3. The population OLS is the linear projection on the span
$\{1,D,X\}$.  Let $\tilde D$ be the linear residual of $D$ after
projection on $1,X$, $\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$.
With $Y=\mu_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)+u$

$$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E\big[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)\big]
   +Cov\!\big(\mu_{0}(X),E[\tilde D\mid X]\big)+\;{\rm terms\; in\;}\tau .$$

$E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$, but $E[\tilde D\mid X]=p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)$
is the non-linear part of the propensity score.  Hence

$$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]
   +Cov\!\big(\mu_{0}(X)-Proj_{1,X}\mu_{0}(X),\,
            p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)\big),$$

and the second term is the linear misspecification bias.  With no
restriction on the functional form of $E[Y(0)\mid X]=\mu_{0}(X)$ or of
$p(X)$ it is unrestricted in sign.

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ with equal mass, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$,
$\mu_{0}(0)=\mu_{0}(2)=0$, $\mu_{0}(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$.
Then $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$,  $Cov(D,X)=0$,
but $Cov(Y,D)<0$ for $M$ large and the population linear projection

$$Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$$

has $\beta_{3}<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.
The same occurs with $p(x)=x^{2}$ and $\mu_{0}(x)=-x^{2}$.

Hence the within-$X$ conditional contrast is positive,
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$, and a fully non-parametric
control for $X$ would give

$$\beta_{np}=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]>0,$$

but the stated linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$ does not guarantee the
sign without a linearity restriction on $E[Y\mid X]$ and $E[D\mid X]$.
With the stated non-parametric conditions the only robust sign
guarantee for the population OLS $D$ coefficient is unconditional
randomisation.

A. Only Case 1.

19.text:
The population coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.  
Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and under the stated conditional
unconfoundedness

$E[Y|X,D]=\mu_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ with $\mu_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., and $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.

* Case 1 $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. With binary $D$
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
With unconditional randomisation the $1+D$ projection is the ATE and
the sign is forced.

* Case 2 $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]
   =E[\mu_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[\mu_{0}(X)|D=0]+E[\tau(X)|D=1]$.
The selection term is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and
$\mu_{0}(x)$ increasing in $X$ the marginal difference in means can be
made negative while $\tau_i>0$ a.s., e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$,
$p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,\mu_{0}(L)=0,\mu_{0}(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. The $Y\sim1+D$ projection is not sign
identified.

* Case 3 $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ and the literal population
linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$ is used. Let $\tilde D$ be the linear
residual of $D$ after projection on $1,X$,
$\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$.
Now
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]+Cov\big(\mu_{0}(X),\tilde D\big)$.
The first term is $>0$ but $Cov(\mu_{0}(X),\tilde D)=
Cov\big(p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X),\mu_{0}(X)-Proj_{1,X}\mu_{0}(X)\big)$
is unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions. With a
non-linear propensity and a non-linear baseline the linear residual is
not orthogonal to $\mu_{0}(X)$. E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable,
$p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $\mu_{0}(0)=\mu_{0}(2)=0,\mu_{0}(1)=M\gg0$,
$\tau\equiv1$, then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$,
$Cov(D,X)=0$, but the linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$
has $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ and $\beta_{3}<0$ for $M$ large.

Hence $E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$ for the non-parametric
residual $D-E[D|X]$, i.e. for a saturated control of $X$, but the
stated linear regression $Y\sim1+D+X$ need not preserve the sign
without a linearity restriction on $E[Y|X]$ and $E[D|X]$. Under the
“no parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’ reading the only
robustly sign-identified population OLS $D$ coefficient is the
unconditionally randomised case.

That is A. Only Case 1.  The textbook statement $E$ is obtained if
“regress Y on $X$’’ is understood as a fully non-parametric control
for $X$, in which case $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ and Case 3 is
sign preserving.

3.text:
With $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., write under conditional
unconfoundedness

$$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X),\qquad 
m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X],\;\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0\;{\rm a.s.},$$

and $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.

*Case 1.* $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))$. For binary $D$
$$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0,$$
the bivariate linear projection is the ATE. The sign is forced.

*Case 2.* $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
 =E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0].$$
$E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but the selection term
$E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted. With
$p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(x)$ increasing in $X$ the bias can
dominate the treatment term, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},\,p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,$
$m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$.
The $1+D$ projection is not sign identified.

*Case 3.*  Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ be the linear residual of
$D$ after projection on $1,X$.  The population OLS coefficient is
$\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$.
With $Y=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)+\eta$,

$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]

E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]\equiv m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X),\qquad
\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0\ {\rm a.s.}
$$

and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.  In particular for every $x$

$$
E[Y\mid D=1,X=x]-E[Y\mid D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0 .
$$

*Case 1.* $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. With a binary $D$ the $1+D$ linear projection is the difference in means

$$
\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0 .
$$

Unconditional randomisation is sign identified.

*Case 2.* $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D$ is in general correlated with $X$. Then

$$
E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]
      +E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0].
$$

The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(x)=P(D=1\mid X=x)$ decreasing in $X$ while $m_{0}(x)=E[Y(0)\mid X=x]$ is increasing, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=M\gg0,\tau\equiv1$, we get $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ regression can be reversed by $X$ selection. Case 2 is not sign protected.

*Case 3.* Now $X$ is in the regression. Let $D^{\perp}$ be the part of $D$ orthogonal to the linear span of $1,X$. By Frisch–Waugh

$$
\beta_{3}= \frac{{\rm Cov}(Y,D^{\perp})}{{\rm Var}(D^{\perp})}.
$$

Conditional on $X$, $E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y\mid X]=E[(D-E[D\mid X])^{2}\mid X]\,\tau(X)$ because $E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y(0)\mid X]=0$ under $D\perp Y(0)\mid X$. Hence

$$
{\rm Cov}(Y,D^{\perp})=E\bigl[{\rm Cov}(Y,D\mid X)\bigr]
   =E\bigl[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\,\tau(X)\bigr]>0,
$$

and ${\rm Var}(D^{\perp})=E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]>0$. Therefore

$$
\beta_{3}= \frac{E\bigl[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\,\tau(X)\bigr]}{E\bigl[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\bigr]}
        =E_{w}\!\left[\tau(X)\right]>0,
$$

a ${\rm Var}(D\mid X)$ weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ average effects $\tau(X)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X]>0$.  Intuitively after partialling out $X$ the residual variation in $D$ is mean independent of $Y(0)$ given $X$, so the only thing left in the numerator is ${\rm Var}(D\mid X)E[\tau\mid X]>0$.

The point is $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $x$. Controlling for pre-income $X$ removes the composition bias that makes Case 2 sign ambiguous and leaves the within-$X$ monotone gain. The population partial association of $D$ with $Y$ after $X$ is therefore necessarily positive.

Hence the $D$ coefficient is guaranteed $>0$ under unconditional randomisation, Case 1, and under conditional randomisation once $X$ is controlled for, Case 3, but not for the uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2.

That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

18.text:
Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i=Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)>0$ a.s. and with
conditional unconfoundedness
$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]\equiv m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$.  With an intercept
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The $1+D$ linear projection is the ATE and is strictly positive.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.  Then
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
      =E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
$E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but the selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-
E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted.  With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$
and $m_{0}(x)$ increasing in $X$ the bias can dominate $\tau$.  E.g.
$X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9$, $p(H)=0.1$, $m_{0}(L)=0$, $m_{0}(H)=100$,
$\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$.  The marginal
$Y\sim1+D$ coefficient is not sign identified.

Case 3.  Let $ \tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ be the linear residual of
$D$ after projection on $1,X$.  Then
$\beta_{3}= {\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)$.
With $Y=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)+\eta$,
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)]
        +{\rm Cov}\big(m_{0}(X),\tilde D\big)+{\rm Cov}\big(p(X)\tau(X),
        \tilde D\big)$,
the first term $>0$ but ${\rm Cov}(m_{0}(X),\tilde D)=
{\rm Cov}\big(m_{0}(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}m_{0}(X),\,p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}
p(X)\big)$ is unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions.
Indeed with $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equal prob., $p(0)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$, we have
${\rm Cov}(D,X)=0$ so ${\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ is constant, $\tilde D=D-
E[D]$, and
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=M/3\,(0.1-0.6333)+{\rm const}<0$ for $M$ large.
Hence the population linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_{D}D+\gamma X+u$
has $\beta_{3}<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

The sign is preserved for the non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$,
$E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]>0$, i.e. for a
saturated control of $X$, but not for the ordinary linear projection
$Y\sim1+D+X$ with no functional form restriction on $m_{0}(X)$ or
$p(X)$.  With the assumptions as stated the only sign guarantee for the
population OLS $D$ coefficient is unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1.

10.text:
With potential outcomes $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and, conditional on $X$,

$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]\equiv\mu_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

*Case 1* $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. For a binary $D$

$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
      =E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$,

the bivariate linear projection is the ATE. The sign is forced.

*Case 2* $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D$ is in general correlated with $X$.
$$
\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
 =E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=0]+E[\tau(X)\mid D=1].
$$
$E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but $E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$
is unrestricted. With $p(x)=P(D=1\mid X=x)$ decreasing in $X$ and
$\mu_{0}(x)$ increasing in $X$, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$,
$\mu_{0}(L)=0,\mu_{0}(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$,
$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The $Y\sim1+D$ population coefficient
can be negative although $\tau_i>0$ a.s.

*Case 3* $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ and $Y$ is linearly projected on
$1,D,X$. Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Then
$\beta_{3}= {\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)$.
Now
${\rm Cov}(Y,D-E[D\mid X])=E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$,
so the non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$ preserves the sign,
$\beta_{np}=E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]>0$.

The linear residual differs from $D-E[D\mid X]$ as soon as
$E[D\mid X]=p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$. With
$E[\tilde D\mid X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$,
$$
{\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)]
+{\rm Cov}\big(\mu_{0}(X),\tilde D\big)
+{\rm Cov}\big(p(X)\tau(X),\tilde D\big),
$$
and ${\rm Cov}(\mu_{0}(X),\tilde D)$ is unrestricted under the stated
non-parametric conditions. 

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ with equal mass,
$p(0)=p(2)=0.9,\;p(1)=0.1$, $\mu_{0}(0)=\mu_{0}(2)=0,\;\mu_{0}(1)=M\gg0$,
$\tau\equiv1$. Then $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$,
${\rm Cov}(D,X)=0$, ${\rm Cov}(Y,X)=0$ and
${\rm Cov}(Y,D)= -0.1778M+0.2333<0$ for $M$ large, so the population
linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_{3}<0$
while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

Hence with no functional-form restriction on $E[Y(0)\mid X]$ and on
$p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$ the linear $1,D,X$ projection can change sign.
The within-$X$ mean difference $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$
is sign preserving for a fully non-parametric control of $X$, i.e. for
the textbook $D-E[D\mid X]$ partial-out. Under the literal linear OLS
projection stated in the question the only robust sign guarantee is
unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

This is the strictly non-parametric guarantee. If $X$ is understood to be
controlled for non-parametrically, the usual textbook statement is that
the within-$X$ partial effect is positive, i.e. Cases 1 and the
non-parametric version of Case 3, E.

public_text.1:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., and under conditional unconfoundedness
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$, $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$
a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. With a binary $D$
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The $1,D$ projection is the ATE.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]+E[\tau(X)|D=1]$.
The selection term is unrestricted.  With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and
$m_{0}(x)$ increasing in $X$ it can dominate $E[\tau(X)|D=1]$, e.g.
$X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$, $m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$,
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.  The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ is not sign identified.

Case 3. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$ and the population linear projection on $1,D,X$
is used. Let $\tilde D$ be the linear residual of $D$ after projection on
$1,X$, $\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$. Then
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X),\tilde D\big)+
Cov\big(p(X)\tau(X),\tilde D\big)$.
The first term $>0$.  $\tilde D$ is the linear residual of $D$ w.r.t.
$X$, i.e. $E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)$.  With no linearity
restriction on $m_{0}(\cdot)$ or $p(\cdot)$ the term
$Cov(m_{0}(X),\tilde D)$ is unrestricted.  It can be made arbitrarily
negative.

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$.  Then
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$, $Cov(D,X)=0$, and the linear
projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$ has $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ for
$M$ large so $\beta_{3}<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s.

The sign preserving quantity is the non-parametric partial out
$Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$, i.e. a saturated control for $X$.
Under the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’ the
strictly linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$ does not preserve the sign.

Hence with the stated non-parametric conditions the only robust sign
guarantee for the population OLS $D$ coefficient is unconditional
randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$ with $\tau_i=Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)>0$ a.s. and under
conditional unconfoundedness

$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

* Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))$. For a binary $D$

$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0,$

the ATE. Unconditional randomisation is sign identified.

* Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
=E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]+E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is free.
With $p(x)=P(D=1\mid X=x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(x)$ increasing in
$X$, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=100,
\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The marginal $1+D$
projection is not sign identified.

* Case 3. The population regression is the linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$.
Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Then $\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]+Cov\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),
E[\tilde D\mid X]\big)$.
The first term is $>0$, but $E[\tilde D\mid X]=p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)$ is the
non-linear part of the propensity. $Cov(m_{0}(X),\tilde D)$ is
unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions. With
$X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equal prob., $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)=0,m_{0}(1)=M\gg0,\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$
for every $x$ but $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ and the linear projection
$Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_{3}<0$. The same
construction works with $m_{0}(X)=X^{2},p(X)=X^{2}$ giving
$\beta_{3}=\tau-1<0$ for $0<\tau<1$.

The strictly positive weighted average 
$E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$ is the coefficient on the
non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$. The stated $1+D+X$ linear
projection uses the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Without a
linearity restriction on $E[Y\mid X]$ and $E[D\mid X]$ the linear
misspecification bias $Cov(m_{0}(X),\tilde D)$ can dominate and flip the
sign.

Hence under the literal linear OLS and no further parametric
assumption the only robustly sign-forced population $D$ coefficient is
unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

If $X$ is understood to be controlled for non-parametrically, $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ and the conventional textbook statement is Cases 1 and 3, i.e. E.

 =E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.

propensity. With $Y=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)+\eta$,
$Cov(Y,D^{\perp})=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X),E[D^{\perp}\mid X]\big)
+...$.
The first term $>0$ but $Cov\big(m_{0}(X),E[D^{\perp}\mid X]\big)$ is unrestricted
under the stated non-parametric conditions.  The linear residual $D^{\perp}$
is not $D-E[D\mid X]$ unless $p(X)$ is linear in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ is linear
in $X$.

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ with equal mass, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$,

on $1,D,X$ has $\beta_{3}<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(d)\mid X$.

Hence the non-parametric within-$X$ contrast $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]
=\tau(X)>0$ is positive, but the linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$ does not
inherit the sign without a linearity restriction on $E[Y\mid X]$ and $E[D\mid X]$.

guarantee for the population OLS $D$ coefficient is unconditional
randomisation.

With potential outcomes $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i=Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)>0$ a.s.
and conditional unconfoundedness

$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,  
$m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s.,  
$p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.

* Case 1. $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$.
For a binary $D$
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The $1+D$ linear projection is the ATE and is strictly positive.

* Case 2. $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
 =E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted.
With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(x)$ increasing in $X$ it can
dominate $E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]$.  e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$.
The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ projection is not sign identified.

* Case 3. $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ and the population linear projection
$Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$ is used. Let $D_{p}={\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$,
$D_{r}=D-D_{p}$. Then

$\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,D_{r})/Var(D_{r})$.

Writing $Y=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)+\eta$,

$Cov(Y,D_{r})=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X),p(X)-D_{p}(X)\big)$

up to $\tau$ terms.  $E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$ but
$E[D_{r}\mid X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\neq0$ whenever $p(X)$ is
non-linear in $X$.  Hence $Cov(m_{0}(X),D_{r})$ is the covariance of the
non-linear part of $m_{0}$ with the non-linear part of $p$ and is
unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions.

$m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)=0,m_{0}(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$, gives

$p(x)=x^{2}$.

The non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$ would give
$\beta^{np}=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$, i.e. the textbook
within-$X$ sign preservation.  With the literal linear regression
$Y\sim1+D+X$ and no parametric restriction on $m_{0}(\cdot)$ or
$p(\cdot)$ the misspecification bias $Cov(m_{0}(X),D_{r})$ can dominate
the positive $E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]$ term.

Hence under the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’
the strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced only by
unconditional randomisation.

      =E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
$E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is
unrestricted. With $p(x)=P(D=1\mid X=x)$ decreasing in $X$ and
$m_{0}(x)$ increasing in $X$ the selection term can dominate the
positive treatment term, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_{0}(L)=0,
m_{0}(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$.

*Case 3* $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ and $Y$ is the linear projection on

$\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,D^{\perp})/Var(D^{\perp})$.
$Cov(Y,D-E[D\mid X])=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$, so the non–parametric
residual $D-E[D\mid X]$ is sign preserving.  The linear residual
$D^{\perp}$ differs from $D-E[D\mid X]$ whenever $E[D\mid X]=p(X)$ is
non-linear in $X$.  Write

$Cov(Y,D^{\perp})=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X),E[D^{\perp}\mid X]\big)
+{\rm remainder}$,

$E[D^{\perp}\mid X]=p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)$ is the non-linear part of the
propensity.  $Cov\big(m_{0}(X),E[D^{\perp}\mid X]\big)$ is unrestricted

$\beta_{3}=\tau-1<0$ for $0<\tau<1$.

Hence the within-$X$ mean difference $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]
=\tau(X)>0$ is positive, i.e. the non-parametric control for $X$ is sign
preserving, but the linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$ is not without an
extra linearity restriction on $E[Y\mid X]$ and $E[D\mid X]$.

With no parametric assumptions beyond those stated the only population
OLS coefficient that is necessarily $>0$ is the unconditionally
randomised difference in means.

Case 1 is sign identified and Case 2 is not, and Case 3 is sign identified.

With potential outcomes $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., the conditional unconfoundedness assumption is
$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_0(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ with $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$ and $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. Then for binary $D$
$\beta_1=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The $1+D$ projection is the ATE.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D$ is generally correlated with $X$.
$\beta_2=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$.
The first term is $>0$ but the selection term $E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted. With pre-income $X$ increasing in $Y(0)$ and $P(D=1\mid X)=p(X)$ decreasing in $X$, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_0(L)=0,m_0(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$, we get $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ regression can be negative even though $\tau_i>0$ a.s.

Case 3. Put $X$ in the regression. Let $\tilde D$ be the part of $D$ orthogonal to the linear span of $1,X$, so by Frisch-Waugh
$\beta_3=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$.
Conditional on $X$, $D\perp Y(0)\mid X$, so
$E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y\mid X]=E[(D-E[D\mid X])^2\mid X]\,\tau(X)$.
Hence
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Cov(Y,D\mid X)]=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$,
and $Var(\tilde D)=E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$.
Thus
$\beta_3=\dfrac{E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]}{E[Var(D\mid X)]}=E_w[\tau(X)]>0$,
a $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ effects $\tau(X)=E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]>0$.

In words, once $X$ is partialled out the residual variation in $D$ is mean independent of any function of $X$. $E[Y(0)\mid X]=m_0(X)$ is fully absorbed by the $X$ regressor, so the only covariance that remains between the $X$-residualised $D$ and $Y$ is the within-$X$ gain $Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)>0$. Controlling for pre-treatment income removes the $X$-selection that reverses Case 2, and the partial association of $D$ with $Y$ inherits the sign of the conditional treatment effect.

So the $D$ coefficient is necessarily $>0$ under unconditional randomisation, Case 1, and under conditional randomisation once $X$ is controlled for, Case 3, whereas the uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2, is not sign protected. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

With $Y = Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., conditional unconfoundedness is
$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]\equiv m_0(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ with $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. For a binary $D$
$\beta_1=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation is the ATE, sign forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D$ is in general correlated with $X$.
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$.
The second term is $X$ selection on the baseline. With $p(x)=P(D=1\mid X=x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(x)$ increasing in $X$, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9$, $p(H)=0.1$, $m_0(L)=0$, $m_0(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$,
$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ regression is not sign identified, the classic Simpson reversal from targeting the jobs programme to low pre-income workers.

Case 3. Add $X$ to the regression. Let $D^{\perp}$ be the part of $D$ orthogonal to $1,X$. By Frisch-Waugh
$\beta_3={\rm Cov}(Y,D^{\perp})/{\rm Var}(D^{\perp})$.
Conditional on $X$,
$E[Y D\mid X]=E[Y\mid X]E[D\mid X]+{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)$
because $E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y(0)\mid X]=0$ under $D\perp Y(0)\mid X$.
Hence
${\rm Cov}(Y,D^{\perp})=E\!\left[{\rm Cov}(Y,D\mid X)\right]
=E\!\left[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)\right]>0$
and
${\rm Var}(D^{\perp})=E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]>0$.
So
$\beta_3=\dfrac{E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)]}{E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]}
=E_w[\tau(X)]>0$,
a ${\rm Var}(D\mid X)$-weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ effects $\tau(X)=E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]>0$.

In words, once pre-treatment income is partialled out the residual variation in $D$ is mean independent of $Y(0)$ given $X$. Within every $X$ stratum $D$ is as good as random and $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$. Controlling for $X$ removes the baseline selection that drives Case 2 and the partial association of $D$ with $Y$ inherits the sign of the within-$X$ treatment gain.

Therefore the population $D$ coefficient is necessarily $>0$ under unconditional randomisation, Case 1, and under conditional randomisation once $X$ is controlled for, Case 3, whereas the uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2, can be negative.

That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

\]

\[
E[\tilde D Y]=E[\tilde D^{2}\tau(X)]+E[\tilde D\mu_{0}(X)],
\]
$E[\tilde D^{2}\tau(X)]>0$ but
$E[\tilde D\mu_{0}(X)]=E[\tilde D(\mu_{0}(X)-P_{1,X}\mu_{0}(X))]$

unconditional randomisation.

$$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0,$$

is sign identified.

$$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
       =E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=0]+E[\tau(X)\mid D=1].$$

$E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but the selection term is unrestricted. With
$p(x)=P(D=1\mid X=x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $\mu_{0}(x)$ increasing in $X$
the bias can dominate the treatment term.  E.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$,
$p(L)=0.9$, $p(H)=0.1$, $\mu_{0}(L)=0$, $\mu_{0}(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$,

$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$

although $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. The $Y\sim1+D$ population OLS is not sign
identified.

$\{1,D,X\}$.  Let $\tilde D$ be the linear residual of $D$ after
projection on $1,X$, $\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$.
With $Y=\mu_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)+u$

$$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E\big[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)\big]
   +Cov\!\big(\mu_{0}(X),E[\tilde D\mid X]\big)+\;{\rm terms\; in\;}\tau .$$

$E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$, but $E[\tilde D\mid X]=p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)$
is the non-linear part of the propensity score.  Hence

$$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]
   +Cov\!\big(\mu_{0}(X)-Proj_{1,X}\mu_{0}(X),\,
            p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)\big),$$

and the second term is the linear misspecification bias.  With no
restriction on the functional form of $E[Y(0)\mid X]=\mu_{0}(X)$ or of

$$Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$$

has $\beta_{3}<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

$$\beta_{np}=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]>0,$$

guarantee for the population OLS $D$ coefficient is unconditional
randomisation.

=E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]+E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]$.

The point is $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $x$. Controlling for pre-income $X$ removes the composition bias that makes Case 2 sign ambiguous and leaves the within-$X$ monotone gain. The population partial association of $D$ with $Y$ after $X$ is therefore necessarily positive.

Hence the $D$ coefficient is guaranteed $>0$ under unconditional randomisation, Case 1, and under conditional randomisation once $X$ is controlled for, Case 3, but not for the uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2.

That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i=Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)>0$ a.s. and with
conditional unconfoundedness
$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]\equiv m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$.  With an intercept
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The $1+D$ linear projection is the ATE and is strictly positive.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.  Then
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
      =E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
$E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but the selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-
E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted.  With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$
and $m_{0}(x)$ increasing in $X$ the bias can dominate $\tau$.  E.g.
$X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9$, $p(H)=0.1$, $m_{0}(L)=0$, $m_{0}(H)=100$,
$\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$.  The marginal
$Y\sim1+D$ coefficient is not sign identified.

Case 3.  Let $ \tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ be the linear residual of
$D$ after projection on $1,X$.  Then
$\beta_{3}= {\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)$.
With $Y=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)+\eta$,
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)]
        +{\rm Cov}\big(m_{0}(X),\tilde D\big)+{\rm Cov}\big(p(X)\tau(X),
        \tilde D\big)$,
the first term $>0$ but ${\rm Cov}(m_{0}(X),\tilde D)=
{\rm Cov}\big(m_{0}(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}m_{0}(X),\,p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}
p(X)\big)$ is unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions.
Indeed with $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equal prob., $p(0)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$, we have
${\rm Cov}(D,X)=0$ so ${\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ is constant, $\tilde D=D-
E[D]$, and
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=M/3\,(0.1-0.6333)+{\rm const}<0$ for $M$ large.
Hence the population linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_{D}D+\gamma X+u$
has $\beta_{3}<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

The sign is preserved for the non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$,
$E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]>0$, i.e. for a
saturated control of $X$, but not for the ordinary linear projection
$Y\sim1+D+X$ with no functional form restriction on $m_{0}(X)$ or
$p(X)$.  With the assumptions as stated the only sign guarantee for the
population OLS $D$ coefficient is unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1.
public_text.10:
With potential outcomes $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and, conditional on $X$,

$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]\equiv\mu_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

*Case 1* $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. For a binary $D$

$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
      =E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$,

the bivariate linear projection is the ATE. The sign is forced.

*Case 2* $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D$ is in general correlated with $X$.
$$
\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
 =E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=0]+E[\tau(X)\mid D=1].
$$
$E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but $E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$
is unrestricted. With $p(x)=P(D=1\mid X=x)$ decreasing in $X$ and
$\mu_{0}(x)$ increasing in $X$, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$,
$\mu_{0}(L)=0,\mu_{0}(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$,
$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The $Y\sim1+D$ population coefficient
can be negative although $\tau_i>0$ a.s.

*Case 3* $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ and $Y$ is linearly projected on
$1,D,X$. Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Then
$\beta_{3}= {\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)$.
Now
${\rm Cov}(Y,D-E[D\mid X])=E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$,
so the non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$ preserves the sign,
$\beta_{np}=E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]>0$.

The linear residual differs from $D-E[D\mid X]$ as soon as
$E[D\mid X]=p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$. With
$E[\tilde D\mid X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$,
$$
{\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)]
+{\rm Cov}\big(\mu_{0}(X),\tilde D\big)
+{\rm Cov}\big(p(X)\tau(X),\tilde D\big),
$$
and ${\rm Cov}(\mu_{0}(X),\tilde D)$ is unrestricted under the stated
non-parametric conditions. 

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ with equal mass,
$p(0)=p(2)=0.9,\;p(1)=0.1$, $\mu_{0}(0)=\mu_{0}(2)=0,\;\mu_{0}(1)=M\gg0$,
$\tau\equiv1$. Then $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$,
${\rm Cov}(D,X)=0$, ${\rm Cov}(Y,X)=0$ and
${\rm Cov}(Y,D)= -0.1778M+0.2333<0$ for $M$ large, so the population
linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_{3}<0$
while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

Hence with no functional-form restriction on $E[Y(0)\mid X]$ and on
$p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$ the linear $1,D,X$ projection can change sign.
The within-$X$ mean difference $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$
is sign preserving for a fully non-parametric control of $X$, i.e. for
the textbook $D-E[D\mid X]$ partial-out. Under the literal linear OLS
projection stated in the question the only robust sign guarantee is
unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

This is the strictly non-parametric guarantee. If $X$ is understood to be
controlled for non-parametrically, the usual textbook statement is that
the within-$X$ partial effect is positive, i.e. Cases 1 and the
non-parametric version of Case 3, E.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential-outcomes model is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau_i$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. Binary $D$ gives $\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$. ATE. Unanimous.

Case 2 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general.
$\beta_2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
Selection term $E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(x)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_0(L)=0,m_0(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Sign not guaranteed. Agreed.

Case 3 is the split.
Non-parametric within-$X$ view: $D^{\perp}_{np}=D-E[D|X]$. Then $Cov(Y,D^{\perp}_{np})=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$ and $\beta_{np}=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]=E_w[\tau(X)]>0$. Within every $x$, $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(x)>0$. Hence textbook statement is Cases 1 and 3 positive, Case 2 not. This is the position of colleagues 11,13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7,9.

Literal linear OLS view: $\beta_3=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Then
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]+Cov(m_0(X),E[\tilde D|X])+...$,
$E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)$. With no linearity restriction on $m_0(\cdot)$ or $p(\cdot)$, $Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)$ is unrestricted. Counterexamples with $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equal prob., $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(0)=m_0(2)=0,m_0(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$, give $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $x$ but $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ and the population linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_3 D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_3<0$. Same with $m_0(x)=x^2$, $p(x)=x^2$. Hence linear misspecification bias can flip sign. This is the position of colleagues 1,10,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8.

The problem explicitly says “Do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given’’ and the regression is the usual linear OLS $Y\sim1+D+X$. Under a strict non-parametric reading the robust guarantee for the population OLS coefficient is only unconditional randomisation. The textbook positive sign for Case 3 requires saturated/non-parametric control for $X$, i.e. the residual $D-E[D|X]$, not the linear residual $D-Proj_{1,X}D$.

Current belief therefore favours A. Only Case 1 is strictly guaranteed. Unresolved nuance remains that if “control for $X$’’ is understood non-parametrically, the usual answer is E. Only Case 1 and Case 3.

11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential outcome set up is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y\mid X,D]=m_0(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ with $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$, $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$, $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$. Then $E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]>0$. OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the mean difference, $\beta_D^1>0$ unconditionally. Agreed by all.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ generally. 
$\beta_D^2=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$.
The selection term can be made arbitrarily negative by letting $p(x)$ be decreasing in $X$ while $m_0(X)$ is increasing. The classic $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$, $m_0(L)=0,m_0(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. Sign not guaranteed. All colleagues agree Case 2 is not sign identified.

Case 3. Regression is the population linear projection on $\{1,D,X\}$. Let $D^{\parallel}=Proj(D\mid1,X)$, $D^{\perp}=D-D^{\parallel}$ and $\beta_D^3=Cov(Y,D^{\perp})/Var(D^{\perp})$.
With $Y=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)+\eta$,
$Cov(Y,D^{\perp})=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]+Cov(m_0(X),E[D^{\perp}\mid X])+...$.
$E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$.
But $E[D^{\perp}\mid X]=p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)$ is the non-linear part of the propensity. $Cov(m_0(X),E[D^{\perp}\mid X])$ is unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions.

Explicit counterexamples given repeatedly:
$X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,$ $p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(0)=m_0(2)=0$, $m_0(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$, gives $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$, $Cov(D,X)=0$, yet the linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_3D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_3<0$ for $M$ large. Same with $p(x)=x^2$, $m_0(x)=-K(x-x^2)$ makes $\beta_D^3$ arbitrarily negative while $\tau>0$ a.s.

The textbook claim that controlling for $X$ restores positivity holds for the non-parametric control $E[Y\mid D,X]$ and for the residual $D-E[D\mid X]$:
$Cov(Y,D-E[D\mid X])=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$ and
$\beta_{np}=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]=E_w[\tau(X)]>0$.
That is the $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ statement used by colleagues 13,14,16,17,21 etc to argue for E: Only Cases 1 and 3.

Under the literal linear OLS interpretation stated in the question and with “do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given”, $E[Y\mid X]$ and $E[D\mid X]$ are not assumed linear in $X$. The linear residual $D^{\perp}$ is not $D-E[D\mid X]$ when $p(X)$ is non-linear, and the misspecification bias $Cov(m_0(X),D^{\perp})$ can dominate the positive $E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]$ term. Hence the population OLS coefficient on $D$ in $Y\sim1+D+X$ can be negative while $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

Therefore under the strict non-parametric reading of the problem the only guaranteed positive population coefficient is unconditional randomisation. Current belief remains A. Only Case 1.

Unresolved tension: the split in the room is between linear-projection vs non-parametric-control interpretation of Case 3. If “regress Y on X” is understood as a saturated / non-parametric control, the usual textbook answer is E: Cases 1 and 3 are sign preserving, Case 2 is not. That interpretation is what the E camp is using. I keep the strict linear OLS interpretation as primary.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The model is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and under the stated conditional unconfoundedness
$E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. For binary $D$
$\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation is sign identified. No dispute.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]+E[\tau(X)|D=1]$.
The selection term $E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted.
With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(x)$ increasing in $X$, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$, $m_0(L)=0,m_0(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.
Marginal $Y\sim1+D$ is not sign identified. Consensus.

Case 3. Population linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$.
Let $P_{1,X}$ be linear projection on $1,X$, $\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$, $\beta_3=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]+Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)+Cov(p(X)\tau(X),\tilde D)$.
$E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$.
$E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-P_{1,X}p(X)$ is the non-linear part of the propensity. 
$Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)=Cov(m_0(X)-P_{1,X}m_0(X),p(X)-P_{1,X}p(X))$ is unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions. The linear residual $\tilde D$ is not $D-E[D|X]$ unless $p(X)$ and $m_0(X)$ are linear in $X$.

Hence sign can flip. E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(0)=m_0(2)=0,m_0(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$, then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$, $Cov(D,X)=0$, yet the linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_3D+\gamma X+u$ has $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ for $M$ large so $\beta_3<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. Also $m_0(X)=X^2$, $p(X)=X^2$ gives $\beta_3=\tau-1<0$ for $0<\tau<1$.

The non-parametric partial out $D-E[D|X]$ does preserve sign:
$Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$, i.e. $\beta_{np}=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$, and $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.
That is the textbook statement that controlling for $X$ restores the sign.

The split in the room is exactly this: colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,21,4,5,6,7,9 argue the textbook non-parametric partial-out interpretation, i.e. answer E, Only Case 1 and Case 3. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,8 argue the literal linear OLS projection with no linearity assumptions on $E[Y|X]$ or $E[D|X]$, i.e. the linear misspecification bias can dominate, so only Case 1 is robustly sign guaranteed, answer A.

Given the explicit instruction “Do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given’’ the regression $Y\sim1+D+X$ is a parametric linear projection and no linearity of $m_0(\cdot)$ or $p(\cdot)$ is allowed. Under that strict reading the only robust sign guarantee for the population OLS $D$ coefficient is unconditional randomisation.

Current best judgment remains A. Only Case 1. If “control for $X$’’ is understood as a fully non-parametric control, the textbook sign-preserving cases are 1 and 3, i.e. E, which is the source of the disagreement.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential outcomes set up is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i=Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)>0$ a.s., and under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp(Y(0),Y(1))$. $\beta_D^1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]>0$. Unconditional randomisation identifies the ATE. Consensus.

Case 2. $D\perp(Y(0),Y(1))|X$ but $D$ can depend on $X$. $\beta_D^2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]+E[\tau(X)|D=1]$. Selection term is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ while $m_0(X)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9$, $p(H)=0.1$, $m_0(L)=0$, $m_0(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Marginal $D$ only regression is not sign-identified. Consensus.

Case 3. $D\perp(Y(0),Y(1))|X$ and $Y$ projected linearly on $1,D,X$. Let $D_p={\rm Proj}(D|1,X)$, $D_r=D-D_p$. $\beta_D^3={\rm Cov}(Y,D_r)/{\rm Var}(D_r)$.

If the non-parametric residual $D^{\perp}=D-E[D|X]$ were used, ${\rm Cov}(Y,D^{\perp})=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$ and $\beta_D^{np}=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$, a ${\rm Var}(D|X)$-weighted average of $\tau(X)>0$. The textbook argument for sign preservation uses this.

With the literal linear projection $D_p$ is linear in $X$ whereas $E[D|X]=p(X)$ is unrestricted. Hence $E[D_r|X]=p(X)-D_p(X)\neq0$ in general and
${\rm Cov}(Y,D_r)=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]+{\rm Cov}\big(m_0(X),p(X)-D_p(X)\big)+\dots$
The second term is the covariance of the non-linear part of $m_0$ with the non-linear part of $p$ and is unrestricted.

Concrete sign reversal: $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(x)=x^2$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|X,D]=x^2+D$ and the linear projection of $Y$ on $1,D,X$ has $\beta_D<0$ while $\tau>0$ a.s. Same with $p(x)=x^2$, $m_0(x)=-x^2$, etc. The linear residual $D_r$ is not orthogonal to a non-linear $m_0(X)$, so misspecification bias $Cov(m_0(X),D_r)$ can dominate the positive $E[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]$.

Current round: Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8 argue the strict linear-projection reading gives A. Only Case 1. Colleagues 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7,9 argue the usual textbook reading in which controlling for $X$ is meant non-parametrically, giving $\beta_3=E_w[\tau(X)]>0$, i.e. E. Only Case 1 and Case 3.

The disagreement is whether “regress Y on 1,D,X” is to be taken as a linear OLS projection with no restriction on $E[Y|X]$ and $E[D|X]$, in which case the linear misspecification bias can flip the sign, or as a saturated control for $X$ which is sign-preserving.

Under the literal statement “do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given” the linear regression itself is the parametric object, and $m_0(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ remain unrestricted. That is enough for the sign reversal in Case 3. Current best judgement under a strict linear-projection interpretation remains A. Only Case 1 must have a positive population $D$ coefficient; Cases 2 and 3 can be made negative with the stated non-parametric conditions. If $X$ is understood as non-parametrically controlled, the textbook answer is E.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The model is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i=Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)>0$ a.s., and under the stated conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ with $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$. 
$\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The $1,D$ population linear projection is the ATE. Sign is forced unconditionally.

Case 2. $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(x)$ increasing in $X$, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_0(L)=0,m_0(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ regression can be negative. All colleagues agree Case 2 is not sign identified.

Case 3. The split is about what “regress $Y$ on $1,D,X$” means.

Non-parametric residual view. Let $D^{*}=D-E[D|X]$. Then 
$Cov(Y,D^{*})=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$ because $E[(D-E[D|X])Y(0)|X]=0$ under unconfoundedness. 
Hence $ \beta_{np}=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]=E_w[\tau(X)]>0$, a positive weighted average of the within-$X$ effects $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$. 
This is the textbook statement that conditioning on $X$ removes the backdoor and the partial effect is positive. This gives the E. Only Case 1 and Case 3 answer, espoused by Colleagues 13,14,16,17,21,2,7,9.

Literal linear projection view. The population OLS coefficient is 
$\beta_3=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$, $E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$. Then
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]+Cov\big(m_0(X),\tilde D\big)+Cov\big(p(X)\tau(X),\tilde D\big)$.
The first term $>0$ but $Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)=Cov(m_0(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}m_0(X),\,p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X))$ is unrestricted under the stated “no parametric assumptions’’ conditions. With a non-linear $p(X)$ and a non-linear $m_0(X)$ the linear residual is not orthogonal to $m_0(X)$.

Explicit counter-examples are given repeatedly: $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(0)=m_0(2)=0,m_0(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$. Then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$, $Cov(D,X)=0$, but $Cov(Y,D)<0$ for $M$ large and the linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_3 D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_3<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(d)|X$. Same with $m_0(X)=X^3$, $p(X)=X^2$. This is the argument of Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8.

Thus under a strictly non-parametric reading with no linearity restriction on $E[Y|X]$ or $E[D|X]$, the linear misspecification bias $Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)$ can dominate $E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]$ and flip the sign. The only robust sign guarantee for the literal population OLS $D$ coefficient is unconditional randomisation, i.e. A. Only Case 1.

The unresolved tension is interpretational: the textbook causal statement is that $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ and a saturated / non-parametric control for $X$ preserves the sign, giving the E. Only Case 1 and Case 3 view. The problem statement says “Do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given’’ and specifies a linear regression $Y\sim1+D+X$. Under that literal OLS definition the linear residual differs from $D-E[D|X]$ and sign reversal is possible, so the strict guarantee is A. Only Case 1.

Current belief remains that with the stated no-parametrics the robust guarantee is Case 1 only; Case 3 is sign preserving only for the non-parametric partial-out $D-E[D|X]$, i.e. for a saturated control, which is the conventional textbook interpretation yielding E.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential-outcomes set-up is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and under the stated conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=\mu_0(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ with $\mu_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp(Y(0),Y(1))|X$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[\mu_0(X)|D=1]-E[\mu_0(X)|D=0]$ .
The selection term is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ while $\mu_0(x)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,\mu_0(L)=0,\mu_0(H)\gg0,\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<E[Y|D=0]=90$. The $1+D$ projection is not sign identified.

Case 3. The literal population linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$ uses $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. 
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]+Cov(\mu_0(X),\tilde D)+...$ . 
The first term $>0$, but $E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$ is the non-linear part of the propensity. $Cov(\mu_0(X),\tilde D)$ is unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions.

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $\mu_0(0)=\mu_0(2)=0,\mu_0(1)=M\gg0,\tau\equiv1$. Under the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’ and taking “regress Y on $1,D,X$’’ literally as the population linear projection, the linear misspecification bias $Cov(\mu_0(X),D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D)$ can be made arbitrarily negative. The sign is therefore forced only by unconditional randomisation.

I remain on the strict linear-projection reading: Only Case 1 is robustly sign guaranteed, A. The split in the room is between this strict reading and the textbook non-parametric control reading which would be E Only Case 1 and Case 3. The disagreement is precisely whether $X$ is controlled for non-parametrically versus linearly.

$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]+Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)+...$.
$E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$ is the textbook non-parametric term $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])>0$.

Room split persists: the textbook non-parametric reading gives Cases 1 and 3 sign preserving, i.e. E Only Case1 and Case3, the strict linear-projection reading gives only Case1 forced, i.e. A Only Case1. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,20,3,4,6,8 argue for A, citing the linear misspecification counterexamples. PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential outcomes set up is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. With binary $D$ the population $1,D$ projection is 
$\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.  
Unconditional randomisation is unanimously sign forced. ATE.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 
$\beta_2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(x)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$, $m_0(L)=0,m_0(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. All colleagues agree the $Y\sim1+D$ coefficient can be negative.

Case 3. Split.

* Textbook / semi-parametric view. Let $D^{\perp np}=D-E[D|X]$. Then 
${\rm Cov}(Y,D^{\perp np})=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$ because $E[(D-E[D|X])Y(0)|X]=0$ under unconfoundedness. Hence 
$\beta^{np}=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D|X)]=E_w[\tau(X)]>0$, a positive weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ effects. This is the argument of colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,4,5,6,7,21: controlling for $X$ removes the $X$-selection that reverses Case 2 and the partial association inherits the sign of $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.

* Strict linear-projection view. The stated regression is the population linear projection on the span $\{1,D,X\}$. Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Then
$\beta_3={\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)$ and
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]+{\rm Cov}\big(m_0(X)+p(X)\tau(X),E[\tilde D|X]\big)$.
$E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$ is the non-linear part of the propensity. The term ${\rm Cov}(m_0(X),E[\tilde D|X])={\rm Cov}\big(m_0(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}m_0(X),\,p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\big)$ is unrestricted under the stated “no parametric assumptions’’ conditions. Counterexamples are repeatedly given: $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(0)=m_0(2)=0,m_0(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$, ${\rm Cov}(D,X)=0$ yet ${\rm Cov}(Y,D)<0$ for large $M$ and the linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_3D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_3<0$. Same with $p(x)=x^2$, $m_0(x)=-x^2$, etc. This is the argument of colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,20,3,8,19.

Hence under the literal OLS interpretation with no linearity of $E[Y|X]$ or $E[D|X]$, the linear misspecification bias ${\rm Cov}\big(m_0(X),D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D\big)$ can dominate the positive $E[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]$ term and flip the sign. The only robustly sign-forced population OLS $D$ coefficient under the stated non-parametric conditions is unconditional randomisation, Case 1, i.e. A. Only Case 1.

If “regress on $X$’’ is understood as a fully non-parametric control for $X$, i.e. the textbook conditioning interpretation, the within-$X$ contrast $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ is preserved and Case 3 is sign-preserving, giving the textbook answer E. Only Case 1 and Case 3. The disagreement in round 2 persists exactly on this linear vs non-parametric control interpretation.
