reflection_text.4:
The potential outcomes set-up is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i=Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)>0$ a.s., conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$, $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. $\beta_D^1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation identifies ATE. Uncontested.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 
$\beta_D^2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
Selection term $E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(x)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_0(L)=0,m_0(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Marginal $Y\sim1+D$ is not sign identified. Consensus.

Case 3. Population linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$. Let $D_p={\rm Proj}(D|1,X)$, $D_r=D-D_p$. 
$\beta_D^3=Cov(Y,D_r)/Var(D_r)$.
Non-parametric residual $D^\perp=D-E[D|X]$ gives $Cov(Y,D^\perp)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$ and $\beta_{np}=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]=E_w[\tau(X)]>0$, the textbook within-$X$ weighted average.

Literal OLS differs: $E[D_r|X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\neq0$. 
$Cov(Y,D_r)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]+Cov\big(m_0(X),p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\big)+\dots$
The second term is $Cov\big(m_0-{\rm Proj}m_0,\;p-{\rm Proj}p\big)$, unrestricted under no linearity restriction on $m_0$ and $p$. Hence linear misspecification bias can dominate.

The set-up is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and under the stated conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=\mu_0(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ with $\mu_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. With an intercept $\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation gives the ATE. All colleagues agree the sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 
$\beta_2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\mu_0(X)|D=1]-E[\mu_0(X)|D=0]+E[\tau(X)|D=1]$.
Selection term is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $\mu_0(x)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$, $\mu_0(L)=0,\mu_0(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ can be negative. Consensus.

Case 3. Literal population OLS $Y\sim1+D+X$. Let $P_{1,X}$ be linear projection, $\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$, $\beta_3=E[\tilde D Y]/E[\tilde D^2]$.
$E[\tilde D Y]=E[\tilde D^2\tau(X)]+E[\tilde D\mu_0(X)]$.
$E[\tilde D^2\tau(X)]>0$ but $E[\tilde D\mu_0(X)]=E[\tilde D(\mu_0(X)-P_{1,X}\mu_0(X))]$ is unrestricted because $\tilde D$ is the linear residual of $D$ w.r.t. $X$ while $\mu_0(X)$ and $p(X)$ can be non-linear.

Standard counter-example: $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $\mu_0(0)=\mu_0(2)=0$, $\mu_0(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$. Then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$, $Cov(D,X)=0$, and the linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_3 D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_3<0$ for $M$ large, i.e. $\beta_3<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. Same with $p(x)=x^2$, $\mu_0(x)=x^2$.

The strictly positive weighted average is for the non-parametric residual:
$E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$, i.e. $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])>0$. That is $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise, so a saturated/non-parametric control of $X$ restores the sign.

The room is split on interpretation of “regress Y on 1,D,X”. 
A camp holds the literal linear OLS reading with no functional-form restriction on $\mu_0(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$. Under that reading the linear misspecification bias $Cov(\mu_0(X),D-P_{1,X}D)$ can be arbitrarily negative, so Cases 2 and 3 can be signed either way and the only robust guarantee is Case 1, A.
The other camp reads “control for X” as non-parametric conditioning, in which case $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ and the partial effect after removing $X$ is a positive weighted average of $\tau(X)$. Under that textbook reading Cases 1 and 3 are sign preserving and Case 2 is not, E.

Given the explicit instruction “Do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given”, the strict linear-projection reading is A. Only Case 1, with the caveat that the usual textbook non-parametric reading gives E. The current round reinforces the split: many colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20 argue for A via the $X\in\{0,1,2\}$/ $p(X)=x^2$ counter-examples; colleagues 13,14,16,17,21 argue for E via Frisch-Waugh and within-X positivity. Unresolved is which interpretation the question setter intends for the phrase “regress Y on a constant, D and X”.
reflection_text.18:
The set-up is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y\mid X,D]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.

Case 1: $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. Binary $D$ gives $\beta_D^1=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation is the ATE, sign forced.

Case 2: $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_D^2=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(x)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$, $m_0(L)=0,m_0(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. Marginal $Y\sim1+D$ is not sign identified.

Case 3: literal population linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$. Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. $\beta_D^3=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]+Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)+\dots$
$E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$ is the non-parametric part $Cov(Y,D-E[D\mid X])>0$.
But $E[\tilde D\mid X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$ is the non-linear part of the propensity, so
$Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)=Cov\big(m_0(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}m_0(X),\,p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\big)$
is unrestricted with no linearity restriction on $m_0$ or $p$. Hence linear misspecification bias can dominate.

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(0)=m_0(2)=0,m_0(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$. Then $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$, $Cov(D,X)=0$, yet $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ for $M$ large and the linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_D D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_D^3<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. Same with $m_0(x)=x^2,p(x)=x^2$ giving $\beta_D=\tau-1<0$ for $0<\tau<1$.

The sign preserving object is the non-parametric partial out $Cov(Y,D-E[D\mid X])=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$, i.e. $\beta_{np}=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$ and $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$. That is the textbook statement that controlling for $X$ preserves sign.

Room split persists. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,20,3,8 argue A Only Case1 for the literal OLS linear projection with no functional form restriction, citing the above linear misspecification counterexamples. Colleagues 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7,9,4 argue E Only Case1 and Case3, identifying the OLS coefficient with the within-$X$ conditional mean difference and treating “regress on $X$” as non-parametric conditioning.

Given the explicit “do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’ and the regression stated as linear $Y\sim1+D+X$, the robust sign guarantee for the population OLS coefficient is unconditional randomisation only. The sign is not guaranteed for Case 2 and, strictly linearly, not guaranteed for Case 3. If “control for $X$” is read as saturated non-parametric control, the textbook answer is Cases 1 and 3.

Current belief remains A Only Case1 as the strictly non-parametric linear-projection guarantee; E is the textbook saturated-control interpretation.

The set-up is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=\mu_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))|X$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$. $\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation identifies the ATE. All agree.

Case 2. $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\mu_0(X)|D=1]-E[\mu_0(X)|D=0]+E[\tau(X)|D=1]$.
Selection on $\mu_0(X)$ via $p(X)$ can dominate. E.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9$, $p(H)=0.1$, $\mu_0(L)=0$, $\mu_0(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Sign not guaranteed. Consensus.

Case 3. Non-parametric partial out: $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$, so
$\beta_{np}=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]=E_w[\tau(X)]>0$.
Within-$X$, $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise. This is the textbook within-$X$ argument used by the E camp.

Literal population OLS $Y\sim1+D+X$: $\beta_3=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$.
Then
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]+Cov(\mu_0(X),\tilde D)+\dots$
$E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$ is the non-linear part of the propensity. With no restriction on $\mu_0(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ the term $Cov(\mu_0(X),\tilde D)$ is unrestricted. Counterexamples are $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $\mu_0(0)=\mu_0(2)=0$, $\mu_0(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$, giving $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ for large $M$ and $\beta_3<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(d)|X$. Same with $p(x)=x^2$, $\mu_0(x)=-x^2$. This is the A camp.

The problem states “Do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given.” That is the strict non-parametric reading, i.e. no linearity of $E[Y|X]$ or $E[D|X]$. Under that literal linear-projection reading the only robust sign guarantee for the population OLS $D$ coefficient is unconditional randomisation, i.e. A. Only Case 1.

If “regress Y on X” is understood as saturated/non-parametric control for $X$, the textbook statement is Cases 1 and 3 positive, Case 2 not, i.e. E. The disagreement in the room is exactly this linear-vs-saturated interpretation.

Current belief remains the strict linear-projection reading: A. Only Case 1, with the caveat that the textbook saturated interpretation yields E.

1.text:
With potential outcomes $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s.,

$E[Y|X,D]=E[Y(0)|X]+D\,E[\tau|X]\equiv m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,

$\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.

For binary $D$,

*Case 1.* $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$.
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The $1,D$ linear projection is the ATE. Sign is forced.

*Case 2.* $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]
 =E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted.
With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(x)$ increasing, e.g. 
$X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$, $m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=100$, 
$\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $\tau_i>0$ a.s.
The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ projection is not sign identified.

*Case 3.* The stated regression is the population OLS linear projection
on $\{1,D,X\}$.  Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Then
$\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ and

$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]
 +Cov\big(m_{0}(X),\tilde D\big)+Cov\big(p(X)\tau(X),\tilde D\big)$.

$E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$ but $E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$ is the
non-linear part of the propensity. Hence

$Cov(m_{0}(X),\tilde D)=Cov\big(m_{0}(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}m_{0}(X),
p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\big)$

is unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions.  $\tilde D\neq
D-E[D|X]$ unless $p(\cdot)$ and $m_{0}(\cdot)$ are linear in $X$.

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)=0,m_{0}(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$, gives
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$, $Cov(D,X)=0$, yet
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ for $M$ large so the linear projection
$Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_{3}<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s.
and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$. The same sign reversal is $m_{0}(x)=x^{2},
p(x)=x^{2}$ giving $\beta_{3}=\tau-1<0$ for $0<\tau<1$.

The sign preserving object is the non-parametric partial out
$Cov\big(Y,D-E[D|X]\big)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$, i.e.
$\beta_{np}=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$ and
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.  That is the textbook saturated
control for $X$.

With the literal linear OLS $Y\sim1+D+X$ and the explicit “no parametric
assumptions beyond what is given’’ reading, the only population OLS $D$
coefficient that is necessarily $>0$ is the unconditionally randomised
one.

A. Only Case 1. 

Remark: if “control for $X$’’ is read as full non-parametric saturation,
$D-E[D|X]$, the textbook statement is Cases 1 and the non-parametric
version of Case 3, i.e. $E$.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The potential-outcomes set-up gives the within-X sign for free. Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$ with $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$. Then

$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]\equiv m_0(X)+D\,\tau(X)$

with $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s. and $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$. Hence for every $x$

$E[Y\mid D=1,X=x]-E[Y\mid D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$,

and conditionally
$Cov(Y,D\mid X)=Var(D\mid X)\,\tau(X)>0$
because $E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y(0)\mid X]=0$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. For binary $D$
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation is the ATE and the $1,D$ difference in means is sign forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D$ is correlated with $X$. Marginally
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The baseline term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted. With a jobs programme targeted to low pre-income, $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ while $m_{0}(x)$ is increasing, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$, $m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, we get $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression is the classic Simpson reversal and is not sign protected.

Case 3. Control for $X$. After partialling out $X$ the $X$-residualised variation in $D$ is mean independent of $Y(0)$ given $X$. In population
$Cov(Y,D-E[D\mid X])=E[Cov(Y,D\mid X)]=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$
and $Var(D-E[D\mid X])=E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$. The Frisch-Waugh partial is
$\beta_{3}=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]=E_{w}[\tau(X)]>0$,
a $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ effects $\tau(X)>0$.

In words, once pre-treatment income is partialled out the residual variation in $D$ is as good as random within each $X$-stratum. Within every stratum the mean gain is $\tau(x)>0$ and controlling for $X$ removes the $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D]$ composition bias that reverses Case 2. The sign of the partial association is inherited from the within-$X$ mean difference.

The three-point $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ U-shaped propensity examples are best-linear-approximation artefacts: they compare the non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$ with its best linear approximation $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. They require a non-monotone propensity in pre-income, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, together with an anti-monotone baseline spike $m_{0}(1)\gg m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)$, i.e. a deliberate mismatch of linear and non-linear parts of $p(\cdot)$ and $m_{0}(\cdot)$. For the economic covariate “income you were making before’’ the economically relevant case is monotone $p(x)$ and monotone $m_{0}(x)$; the construction is a measure-zero linear-misspecification curiosity, not a sign reversal of the within-$X$ conditional mean effect that the regression on $X$ is intended to recover.

Hence the $D$ coefficient is necessarily $>0$ under unconditional randomisation, Case 1, and under conditional randomisation once $X$ is controlled for, Case 3, whereas the uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2, can be reversed by selection on $X$. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

3.text:
With potential outcomes $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s.,

$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]\equiv m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.

Then for every $x$
$E[Y\mid D=1,X=x]-E[Y\mid D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$.

$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The $1,D$ linear projection is the ATE. Sign forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.

$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]

$p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$,

Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Then $\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$
and

$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]
 +Cov\!\big(m_{0}(X),\tilde D\big)+Cov\!\big(p(X)\tau(X),\tilde D\big)$,

Hence
$Cov\big(Y,D-E[D\mid X]\big)=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$,
i.e. the non-parametric within-$X$ contrast $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]

$Y\sim1+D+X$ does not inherit the sign without a linearity restriction on
$E[Y\mid X]$ and $E[D\mid X]$. The linear misspecification bias
$Cov(m_{0}(X),\tilde D)$ can dominate $E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]$ and flip the
sign.

With the “no parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’ reading and
the regression taken literally as the population OLS linear projection,
the only robustly sign-forced $D$ coefficient is the unconditionally
randomised difference in means.

A. Only Case 1

Remark: this is the literal OLS statement. If “control for $X$’’ is
understood non-parametrically as saturated control, $D-E[D\mid X]$,
then $\beta_{np}=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$ and the

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Write the potential outcomes as $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s. Under the conditional unconfoundedness that is part of the set-up

$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]\equiv m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,

$m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.

Hence point-wise

$E[Y\mid D=1,X=x]-E[Y\mid D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$.

$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.

Unconditional randomisation is the ATE and the $1,D$ linear projection is sign forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general.

$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
 =E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.

$E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is free. With a jobs programme targeted to low pre-income, $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ while $m_{0}(x)$ is increasing, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$, $m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$,

$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$

although $\tau_i>0$ a.s. The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ regression is the classic Simpson reversal and is not sign protected.

Case 3. Now $X$ is partialled out. Conditional on $X$

$E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y\mid X]=E[(D-E[D\mid X])^{2}\mid X]\,\tau(X)$

because $E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y(0)\mid X]=0$ under $D\perp Y(0)\mid X$. Hence

$Cov(Y,D-E[D\mid X])=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$,

$Var(D-E[D\mid X])=E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$,

and by Frisch–Waugh the partial association of $D$ with $Y$ after $X$ is

$\beta_{3}^{*}=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]
      =E_{w}[\tau(X)]>0$,

a $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ effects $\tau(X)$.

In words, after partialling out pre-treatment income the residual variation in $D$ is mean independent of $Y(0)$ given $X$. Within every $X$ stratum $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ and the only covariance that survives between the $X$-residualised $D$ and $Y$ is $Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)>0$. Controlling for $X$ removes the $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D]$ composition bias that reverses Case 2.

The three-point $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$ with a spike $m_{0}(1)=M\gg0$ examples are exactly the linear-misspecification artefact of comparing the non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$ with its best linear approximation $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. They require a U-shaped, non-monotone propensity in pre-income together with an opposite non-monotone baseline and $Cov(D,X)=0$, $Cov(Y,X)=0$ simultaneously. For the economic covariate “income you were making before’’ the relevant case is monotone $p(x)$ decreasing and monotone $m_{0}(x)$ increasing; the pathological cancellation is a measure-zero curiosity rather than the population implied by the question. Under the usual causal reading of “regress $Y$ on $1,D,X$”, i.e. conditioning on $X$, the sign is inherited from the within-$X$ contrast.

So the $D$ coefficient is necessarily $>0$ under unconditional randomisation, Case 1, and under conditional randomisation once $X$ is controlled for, Case 3, whereas the uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2, can be reversed by selection on $X$. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

 =E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The selection term is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and
$m_{0}(x)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9$, $p(H)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(L)=0$, $m_{0}(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$,

$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$

although $\tau_i>0$ a.s. The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ projection is not sign
identified.

*Case 3.* The stated regression is the population linear projection
$Y\sim1+D+X$, $\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with
$\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Then

$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]
 +Cov\big(m_{0}(X),\tilde D\big)+\dots$,

$E[\tilde D\mid X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$.

$E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$ is the non-parametric within-$X$ term
$Cov\big(Y,D-E[D\mid X]\big)$.  With no linearity restriction on
$m_{0}(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$,

$Cov\big(m_{0}(X),\tilde D\big)=
Cov\big(m_{0}(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}m_{0}(X),\,
p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\big)$

is unrestricted. $D^{\perp}=D-E[D\mid X]$ is sign preserving,
$Cov(Y,D-E[D\mid X])=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$, but
$D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D\neq D-E[D\mid X]$ as soon as $p(X)$ is non-linear.

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable,
$p(0)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$.
Then $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$,
$Cov(D,X)=0$, yet $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ for $M$ large and the linear
projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_{3}<0$ while
$Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.
The same occurs with $m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$, $p(x)=x^{2}$ giving
$\beta_{3}=\tau-1<0$ for $0<\tau<1$.

Hence with no parametric shape imposed on $E[Y\mid X]$ and $E[D\mid X]$
the linear misspecification bias $Cov\big(m_{0}(X),D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D\big)$
can dominate $E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]$ and flip the sign. The only
population OLS $D$ coefficient that is necessarily $>0$ under the stated
non-parametric conditions is unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1.

Remark: the non-parametric partial out $D-E[D\mid X]$ is sign preserving,
$E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$, i.e. the textbook
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$. That is the usual
Cases 1 and saturated Case 3 statement.

18.text:
With potential outcomes $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s. and

$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s.,  
$D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$,

the population objects asked for are the population linear projections.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$.  For binary $D$
$$
\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0,
$$
the $1,D$ linear projection is the ATE. Sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general.
$$
\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]
          +E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0].
$$
$E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but the selection term is free.  With $p(x)$
decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(x)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$,
$p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$, $m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$,
$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$ although $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s.  The
marginal $Y\sim1+D$ projection is not sign identified.

Case 3. The stated regression is the literal population OLS
$Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$.  Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$.
$$
\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D),\qquad 
E[\tilde D\mid X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X).
$$
Now
$$
Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]
 +Cov\!\big(m_{0}(X),\tilde D\big)+Cov\!\big(p(X)\tau(X),\tilde D\big),
$$
and
$$
Cov\big(m_{0}(X),\tilde D\big)=Cov\!\Big(m_{0}(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}m_{0}(X),\,
p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\Big)
$$
is unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions.  $E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$ is the non-parametric term $Cov(Y,D-E[D\mid X])>0$, but
$\tilde D\neq D-E[D\mid X]$ as soon as $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$.

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$.  Then
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$, $Cov(D,X)=0$, yet
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ for $M$ large and the linear projection
$Y\sim1+D+X$ has $\beta_{3}<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. and
$D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.  The same sign reversal is $m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$,
$p(x)=x^{2}$, $\beta_{3}=\tau-1<0$ for $0<\tau<1$.

Hence the sign preserving object is the non-parametric partial out
$Cov(Y,D-E[D\mid X])=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$, i.e.
$\beta_{np}=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$ and
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.
With the literal linear OLS $Y\sim1+D+X$ and no linearity restriction
on $E[Y\mid X]$ and $E[D\mid X]$ the linear misspecification bias
$Cov(m_{0}(X),\tilde D)$ can dominate the positive within-$X$ term.

Under the strict “no parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’
reading of the stated linear regressions, the only robustly sign forced
population OLS $D$ coefficient is unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

Remark: if “control for $X$’’ is read as a fully saturated,
non-parametric control, $D-E[D\mid X]$, the usual textbook statement is
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ and Cases 1 and the saturated
version of Case 3 are sign preserving, the $E$ camp.

19.text:
With $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$

$$
E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]\equiv m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X),
\qquad \tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0~{\rm a.s.}
$$

so that for every $x$

$E[Y\mid D=1,X=x]-E[Y\mid D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$.

* Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$

$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The $1,D$ linear projection is the ATE. Sign is forced.

* Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $D\not\perp X$ in general

$$
\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
=E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0] .
$$

The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is free.
With $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing,
e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$, $m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=100$,
$\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$ although $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s.
The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ projection is not sign identified.

* Case 3. Literal population OLS $Y\sim1+D+X$.
Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Then $\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ and

$$
Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X),\tilde D\big)+\dots,
\qquad E[\tilde D\mid X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X).
$$

$E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$ but $E[\tilde D\mid X]$ is the non-linear part of
the propensity. Hence

$Cov(m_{0}(X),\tilde D)=Cov\big(m_{0}(X)-Proj_{1,X}m_{0}(X),
p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)\big)$

is unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions. $D^{\perp}=
D-E[D\mid X]\neq D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ as soon as $p(\cdot)$ is non-linear.
E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)=0,m_{0}(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$, gives
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0\;\forall x$, $Cov(D,X)=0$, yet
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ for $M$ large and the linear projection
$Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_{3}<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s.
and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$. The same occurs with $m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$,
$p(x)=x^{2}$ giving $\beta_{3}=\tau-1<0$ for $0<\tau<1$.

The sign preserving object is the non-parametric partial out
$Cov\big(Y,D-E[D\mid X]\big)=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$, i.e.
$\beta_{np}=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]=E_{w}[\tau(X)]>0$.
With the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’ the
literal linear OLS $1+D+X$ can be flipped by the linear-misspecification
bias $Cov\big(m_{0}(X),D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D\big)$.

Hence under the literal linear-projection reading the only robustly sign
forced population $D$ coefficient is unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1.

Remark: if “regress on $X$’’ is read as fully saturated/non-parametric
control, i.e. $D-E[D\mid X]$, then $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$
pointwise and the textbook statement is Cases 1 and the non-parametric
version of Case 3, the $E$ camp.

17.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the textbook within-X reading is the right reading of the question and it gives us Cases 1 and 3 with Case 2 the classic Simpson reversal.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and with the conditional unconfoundedness that is part of the set up

$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]\equiv m_0(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,

$m_0(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.

Hence for every $x$

$E[Y\mid D=1,X=x]-E[Y\mid D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$.

Case 1 is immediate. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$ so with a binary $D$

$\beta_1=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.

Unconditional randomisation is the ATE.

Case 2 is the selection problem. Marginally

$\beta_2=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
 =E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$.

$E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but $E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$ is free. With pre-income $X$ increasing $m_0$ and a jobs programme targeted to low $X$, $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$, the baseline term can dominate the treatment term. E.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$, $m_0(L)=0,m_0(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression is not sign protected.

Case 3 controls for $X$. Conditional on $X$

$Cov(Y,D\mid X)=Var(D\mid X)\,\tau(X)>0$,

because $E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y(0)\mid X]=0$ under $D\perp Y(0)\mid X$. Hence

$Cov\big(Y,D-E[D\mid X]\big)=E[Cov(Y,D\mid X)]=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$.

By Frisch-Waugh the population partial that is obtained after removing $X$ is

$\beta_{3}= \frac{E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]}{E[Var(D\mid X)]}
       =E_{w}[\tau(X)]>0$,

a $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ effects $\tau(X)$. After partialling out pre-treatment income the residual variation in $D$ is mean independent of $Y(0)$ given $X$. Within every $X$ stratum $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$, so the only thing that survives in the numerator is $Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)>0$. Controlling for $X$ removes the $E[m_0(X)\mid D]$ composition bias that reverses Case 2 and leaves the within-$X$ gain.

The three-point $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$ with a spike $m_0(1)=M\gg0$ constructions that are quoted for Case 3 are a best-linear-approximation artefact: they conflate the non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$ with its best linear approximation $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. They require a U-shaped, non-monotone propensity in pre-income together with a non-monotone baseline that spikes exactly where the propensity is low, and they need $Cov(D,X)=0$ and $Cov(Y,X)=0$ simultaneously. For the economic variable “income you were making before’’ the relevant case is monotone $p(x)$ decreasing and monotone $m_0(x)$ increasing. In that monotone, and in the usual causal reading of “regress $Y$ on $1,D,X$’’ i.e. conditioning on $X$ to remove selection, the within-$X$ contrast $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ is preserved pointwise and the population partial association of $D$ with $Y$ after $X$ inherits that sign.

So the $D$ coefficient is necessarily $>0$ under unconditional randomisation, Case 1, and under conditional randomisation once $X$ is controlled for, Case 3, whereas the uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2, can be reversed by selection on $X$. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

21.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$ with $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and with the conditional unconfoundedness that is part of the set-up

$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]\equiv m_0(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.

Hence for every $x$

$E[Y\mid D=1,X=x]-E[Y\mid D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$,

the within-$X$ mean gain is strictly positive and
$Cov(Y,D\mid X)=Var(D\mid X)\,\tau(X)>0$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. With a binary $D$
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation is the ATE.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D$ is generally dependent on $X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
=E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$.
$E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but $E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$ is free.
With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(x)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$ increasing in $X$,
e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_0(L)=0,m_0(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$,
$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The raw $Y\sim1+D$ regression is the
classic Simpson reversal and is not sign protected.

Case 3. Now $X$ is controlled for. Conditional on $X$,
$E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y\mid X]=E[(D-E[D\mid X])^{2}\mid X]\,\tau(X)$
because $E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y(0)\mid X]=0$ under $D\perp Y(0)\mid X$.
Hence

$Cov(Y,D-E[D\mid X])=E[Cov(Y,D\mid X)]=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$,

$Var(D-E[D\mid X])=E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$ and the Frisch-Waugh partial for $D$
after $X$ is

$\beta_{np}=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]
=E_{w}[\tau(X)]>0,$

a $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$
effects $\tau(X)>0$. In words, after partialling out pre-treatment income
the residual variation in $D$ is mean independent of $Y(0)$ given $X$,
so the only thing that survives in the numerator is $Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)>0$.
Controlling for $X$ removes the $E[m_0(X)\mid D]$ composition bias that
reverses Case 2 and the partial association of $D$ with $Y$ inherits the
sign of the conditional gain.

The $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ U-shaped propensity examples, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9$,
$p(1)=0.1$ with a spike $m_0(1)=M\gg0$, are the usual linear-misspecification
curiosities. They are constructed so that $Cov(D,X)=0$, $Cov(Y,X)=0$ and the
best linear approximation to $p(X)$ and to $m_0(X)$ is essentially flat,
so the linear residual $D- Proj_{1,X}D$ is $D-E[D]$ and no control for $X$
is actually exercised. The construction needs a non-monotone propensity
in pre-income and a baseline $m_0(X)$ that spikes in the opposite way,
with the propensity high at the two extremes of income and low in the
middle. For the economic variable “income you were making before’’ the
relevant case is monotone $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and monotone
$m_0(x)$ increasing in $X$. Under the stated conditional unconfoundedness
the non-parametric within-$X$ contrast $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$
is positive pointwise, and the population partial effect of $D$ after
controlling for $X$ is the positive weighted average of those within-$X$
effects.

Hence the $D$ coefficient is necessarily $>0$ under unconditional
randomisation, Case 1, and under conditional randomisation once $X$ is
controlled for, Case 3, whereas the uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression
under conditional randomisation, Case 2, can be reversed by selection on
$X$. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D$ is correlated with $X$. Marginally
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The baseline term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted. With a jobs programme targeted to low pre-income, $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ while $m_{0}(x)$ is increasing, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$, $m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, we get $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression is the classic Simpson reversal and is not sign protected.

Case 3. Control for $X$. After partialling out $X$ the $X$-residualised variation in $D$ is mean independent of $Y(0)$ given $X$. In population
$Cov(Y,D-E[D\mid X])=E[Cov(Y,D\mid X)]=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$
and $Var(D-E[D\mid X])=E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$. The Frisch-Waugh partial is
$\beta_{3}=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]=E_{w}[\tau(X)]>0$,
a $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ effects $\tau(X)>0$.

In words, once pre-treatment income is partialled out the residual variation in $D$ is as good as random within each $X$-stratum. Within every stratum the mean gain is $\tau(x)>0$ and controlling for $X$ removes the $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D]$ composition bias that reverses Case 2. The sign of the partial association is inherited from the within-$X$ mean difference.

The three-point $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ U-shaped propensity examples are best-linear-approximation artefacts: they compare the non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$ with its best linear approximation $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. They require a non-monotone propensity in pre-income, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, together with an anti-monotone baseline spike $m_{0}(1)\gg m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)$, i.e. a deliberate mismatch of linear and non-linear parts of $p(\cdot)$ and $m_{0}(\cdot)$. For the economic covariate “income you were making before’’ the economically relevant case is monotone $p(x)$ and monotone $m_{0}(x)$; the construction is a measure-zero linear-misspecification curiosity, not a sign reversal of the within-$X$ conditional mean effect that the regression on $X$ is intended to recover.

Hence the $D$ coefficient is necessarily $>0$ under unconditional randomisation, Case 1, and under conditional randomisation once $X$ is controlled for, Case 3, whereas the uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2, can be reversed by selection on $X$. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

With potential outcomes $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0\;a.s.$, the
conditional unconfoundedness that is part of the set up is

$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]\equiv m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,
$m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s.,
$p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$ and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

The population objects quoted are population linear projections.

Case 1.  $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. For binary $D$

$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$,

the $1,D$ projection is the ATE.  Sign forced.

Case 2.  $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general.

$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
=E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.

$E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is
unrestricted.  With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(x)$ increasing,
e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1$, $m_{0}(L)=0,m_{0}(H)=100$,
$\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$ although $\tau_i>0$ a.s.
The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ projection is not sign identified.

Case 3. The stated regression is the ordinary linear projection on the
span $\{1,D,X\}$.  Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$,
$\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$.  Then

$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]
+Cov\big(m_{0}(X),\tilde D\big)+Cov\big(p(X)\tau(X),\tilde D\big)$,

$E[\tilde D\mid X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$ is the non-linear part of
the propensity.  Hence

$Cov(m_{0}(X),\tilde D)=Cov\big(m_{0}(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}m_{0}(X),
p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\big)$

is unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions.  The linear
residual $\tilde D$ is not $D-E[D\mid X]$ unless $p(\cdot)$ and
$m_{0}(\cdot)$ are linear in $X$.

$p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=m_{0}(2)=0,m_{0}(1)=M\gg0$,
$\tau\equiv1$.  Then $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $x$,

linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_{3}<0$
while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.  The same sign
reversal is obtained with $m_{0}(x)=x^{2},p(x)=x^{2}$ giving

$Cov\big(Y,D-E[D\mid X]\big)=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$,

sign forced $D$ coefficient is unconditional randomisation.

$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]\equiv m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,

$m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.

$E[Y\mid D=1,X=x]-E[Y\mid D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$.

$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.

Unconditional randomisation is the ATE and the $1,D$ linear projection is sign forced.

$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]

Controlling for $X$ removes the $E[m_0(X)\mid D]$ composition bias that reverses Case 2 and leaves the within-$X$ gain.

The three-point $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$ with a spike $m_0(1)=M\gg0$ constructions that are quoted for Case 3 are a best-linear-approximation artefact: they conflate the non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$ with its best linear approximation $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. They require a U-shaped, non-monotone propensity in pre-income together with a non-monotone baseline that spikes exactly where the propensity is low, and they need $Cov(D,X)=0$ and $Cov(Y,X)=0$ simultaneously. For the economic variable “income you were making before’’ the relevant case is monotone $p(x)$ decreasing and monotone $m_0(x)$ increasing. In that monotone, and in the usual causal reading of “regress $Y$ on $1,D,X$’’ i.e. conditioning on $X$ to remove selection, the within-$X$ contrast $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ is preserved pointwise and the population partial association of $D$ with $Y$ after $X$ inherits that sign.

So the $D$ coefficient is necessarily $>0$ under unconditional randomisation, Case 1, and under conditional randomisation once $X$ is controlled for, Case 3, whereas the uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2, can be reversed by selection on $X$. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$ with $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and with the conditional unconfoundedness that is part of the set-up

$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y(0)\mid X]+D\,E[\tau\mid X]\equiv m_0(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.

Hence for every $x$

$E[Y\mid D=1,X=x]-E[Y\mid D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$,

the within-$X$ mean gain is strictly positive and
$Cov(Y,D\mid X)=Var(D\mid X)\,\tau(X)>0$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. With a binary $D$
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation is the ATE.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D$ is generally dependent on $X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
=E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$.
$E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but $E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$ is free.
With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(x)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$ increasing in $X$,
e.g. $X\in\{L,H\}$, $p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_0(L)=0,m_0(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$,
$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The raw $Y\sim1+D$ regression is the
classic Simpson reversal and is not sign protected.

Case 3. Now $X$ is controlled for. Conditional on $X$,
$E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y\mid X]=E[(D-E[D\mid X])^{2}\mid X]\,\tau(X)$
because $E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y(0)\mid X]=0$ under $D\perp Y(0)\mid X$.
Hence

$Cov(Y,D-E[D\mid X])=E[Cov(Y,D\mid X)]=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]>0$,

$Var(D-E[D\mid X])=E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$ and the Frisch-Waugh partial for $D$
after $X$ is

$\beta_{np}=E[Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]
=E_{w}[\tau(X)]>0,$

a $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$
effects $\tau(X)>0$. In words, after partialling out pre-treatment income
the residual variation in $D$ is mean independent of $Y(0)$ given $X$,
so the only thing that survives in the numerator is $Var(D\mid X)\tau(X)>0$.
Controlling for $X$ removes the $E[m_0(X)\mid D]$ composition bias that
reverses Case 2 and the partial association of $D$ with $Y$ inherits the
sign of the conditional gain.

The $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ U-shaped propensity examples, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9$,
$p(1)=0.1$ with a spike $m_0(1)=M\gg0$, are the usual linear-misspecification
curiosities. They are constructed so that $Cov(D,X)=0$, $Cov(Y,X)=0$ and the
best linear approximation to $p(X)$ and to $m_0(X)$ is essentially flat,
so the linear residual $D- Proj_{1,X}D$ is $D-E[D]$ and no control for $X$
is actually exercised. The construction needs a non-monotone propensity
in pre-income and a baseline $m_0(X)$ that spikes in the opposite way,
with the propensity high at the two extremes of income and low in the
middle. For the economic variable “income you were making before’’ the
relevant case is monotone $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and monotone
$m_0(x)$ increasing in $X$. Under the stated conditional unconfoundedness
the non-parametric within-$X$ contrast $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$
is positive pointwise, and the population partial effect of $D$ after
controlling for $X$ is the positive weighted average of those within-$X$
effects.

Hence the $D$ coefficient is necessarily $>0$ under unconditional
randomisation, Case 1, and under conditional randomisation once $X$ is
controlled for, Case 3, whereas the uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression
under conditional randomisation, Case 2, can be reversed by selection on
$X$. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential-outcomes model is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau_i$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. For binary $D$, $\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation gives the ATE. Unanimous.

Case 2 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general. $\beta_2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$. Selection term is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(x)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_0(L)=0,m_0(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Sign not guaranteed. Agreed.

Case 3 split between non-parametric within-$X$ reading and literal linear OLS reading.

Non-parametric within-$X$ reading: $D^{\perp}_{np}=D-E[D|X]$. Then $Cov(Y,D^{\perp}_{np})=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$ and $\beta_{np}=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]=E_w[\tau(X)]>0$. Within every $x$, $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(x)>0$. This is the textbook statement Cases 1 and 3 positive, Case 2 not. Position of colleagues 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7,9.

Literal linear OLS reading: $\beta_3=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Then $Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]+Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)+\dots$, $E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$. With no linearity restriction on $m_0(\cdot)$ or $p(\cdot)$, $Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)$ is unrestricted. Counterexamples with $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(0)=m_0(2)=0,m_0(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$, give $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $x$ but $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ and the population linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_3 D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_3<0$. Same with $m_0(x)=x^2$, $p(x)=x^2$. This is the position of colleagues 1,10,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8.

The problem explicitly says “Do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given’’ and the regression is the usual linear OLS $Y\sim1+D+X$. Under a strict non-parametric reading the robust guarantee for the population OLS coefficient is only unconditional randomisation. The textbook positive sign for Case 3 requires saturated/non-parametric control for $X$, i.e. the residual $D-E[D|X]$, not the linear residual $D-Proj_{1,X}D$.

Current belief therefore favours A. Only Case 1 is strictly guaranteed for the literal linear projection. The unresolved nuance remains that if “control for $X$’’ is understood non-parametrically, the usual answer is E. Only Case 1 and Case 3. Majority of current round 4 still leans A with remark about E.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The model is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. $\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation is sign identified, no dispute.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$. $\beta_2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$. Selection term unrestricted. Example $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$, $m_0(x)$ increasing in $X$, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_0(L)=0,m_0(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Marginal $Y\sim1+D$ is not sign identified. Consensus.

Case 3. Population linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$. $\beta_3=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. $Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]+Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)+Cov(p(X)\tau(X),\tilde D)$. $E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$. $E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$ is the non-linear part of propensity. $Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)=Cov(m_0(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}m_0(X),p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X))$ unrestricted under non-parametric conditions. $\tilde D\neq D-E[D|X]$ unless $p(\cdot),m_0(\cdot)$ linear.

Sign flip examples: $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(0)=m_0(2)=0,m_0(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0\;\forall x$, $Cov(D,X)=0$, yet $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ for $M$ large so linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_3D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_3<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. Also $m_0(x)=x^2,p(x)=x^2$ gives $\beta_3=\tau-1<0$ for $0<\tau<1$.

Sign-preserving object is non-parametric partial out $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$, i.e. $\beta_{np}=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$ and $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.

Split in room persists: 13,14,16,17,2,4,5,6,7,9,21 argue textbook saturated control reading, i.e. answer E Only Case1 and Case3, appealing to monotone $p(x),m_0(x)$ for pre-income and to $Cov(Y,D^\perp)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,8 argue literal linear OLS projection with no linearity assumptions on $E[Y|X]$ or $E[D|X]$, i.e. $Y\sim1+D+X$ is parametric linear and misspecification bias can dominate, so only Case1 is robustly sign guaranteed, answer A.

Given explicit instruction “Do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given”, the regression $Y\sim1+D+X$ is a parametric linear projection and no linearity of $m_0(\cdot)$ or $p(\cdot)$ is allowed. Under that strict reading the only robust sign guarantee for the population OLS $D$ coefficient is unconditional randomisation.

Current best judgment remains A. Only Case1. If “control for $X$’’ is understood as fully non-parametric saturated control, the textbook sign-preserving cases are 1 and 3, i.e. E, which remains the source of the unresolved intent disagreement.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION:

$E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$ is the non-parametric within-$X$ part $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])>0$.
$E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$ is the non-linear part of the propensity, so
$Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)=Cov\big(m_0(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}m_0(X),\,p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\big)$
is unrestricted with no linearity restriction on $m_0$ or $p$.
Hence $D^{\perp}=D-E[D|X]\neq D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ as soon as $p(\cdot)$ is non-linear.

Counterexamples:
* $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(0)=m_0(2)=0,m_0(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$. Then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0\;\forall x$, $Cov(D,X)=0$, yet $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ for $M$ large and the linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_3D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_3<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$.
* $m_0(x)=x^2$, $p(x)=x^2$ gives $\beta_3=\tau-1<0$ for $0<\tau<1$.

Sign preserving object is the non-parametric partial out
$Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$, i.e. $\beta_{np}=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$ and $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.

Split persists:
A camp 1,10,11,12,15,18,20,3,8 : literal OLS linear projection with no parametric shape => only Case1 is robustly sign forced; Case3 can be flipped by linear misspecification bias.
E camp 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7,9,4 : ‘control for X’ read as saturation / conditioning, so $D-E[D|X]$ is sign preserving and Cases1 and 3 are guaranteed, Case2 not.

Current belief remains A. Only Case1 as the strictly non-parametric linear-projection guarantee under the stated “do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’ and the regression stated as linear $Y\sim1+D+X$. E is the textbook saturated-control interpretation $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])>0$. Unresolved is whether the question intends the saturated non-parametric control or the literal best linear approximation.

reflection_text.8:
The potential-outcomes model is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau_i$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. For binary $D$, $\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation gives the ATE. Unanimous.

Case 2 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general. $\beta_2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$. Selection term is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(x)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_0(L)=0,m_0(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Sign not guaranteed. Agreed.

Case 3 split between non-parametric within-$X$ reading and literal linear OLS reading.

Non-parametric within-$X$ reading: $D^{\perp}_{np}=D-E[D|X]$. Then $Cov(Y,D^{\perp}_{np})=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$ and $\beta_{np}=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]=E_w[\tau(X)]>0$. Within every $x$, $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(x)>0$. This is the textbook statement Cases 1 and 3 positive, Case 2 not. Position of colleagues 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7,9.

Literal linear OLS reading: $\beta_3=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Then $Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]+Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)+\dots$, $E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$. With no linearity restriction on $m_0(\cdot)$ or $p(\cdot)$, $Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)$ is unrestricted. Counterexamples with $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(0)=m_0(2)=0,m_0(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$, give $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $x$ but $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ and the population linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_3 D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_3<0$. Same with $m_0(x)=x^2$, $p(x)=x^2$. This is the position of colleagues 1,10,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8.

The problem explicitly says “Do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given’’ and the regression is the usual linear OLS $Y\sim1+D+X$. Under a strict non-parametric reading the robust guarantee for the population OLS coefficient is only unconditional randomisation. The textbook positive sign for Case 3 requires saturated/non-parametric control for $X$, i.e. the residual $D-E[D|X]$, not the linear residual $D-Proj_{1,X}D$.

Current belief therefore favours A. Only Case 1 is strictly guaranteed for the literal linear projection. The unresolved nuance remains that if “control for $X$’’ is understood non-parametrically, the usual answer is E. Only Case 1 and Case 3. Majority of current round 4 still leans A with remark about E.

The model is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. $\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation is sign identified, no dispute.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$. $\beta_2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$. Selection term unrestricted. Example $p(x)$ decreasing in $X$, $m_0(x)$ increasing in $X$, e.g. $X\in\{L,H\},p(L)=0.9,p(H)=0.1,m_0(L)=0,m_0(H)=100,\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Marginal $Y\sim1+D$ is not sign identified. Consensus.

Case 3. Population linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$. $\beta_3=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. $Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]+Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)+Cov(p(X)\tau(X),\tilde D)$. $E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$. $E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$ is the non-linear part of propensity. $Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)=Cov(m_0(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}m_0(X),p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X))$ unrestricted under non-parametric conditions. $\tilde D\neq D-E[D|X]$ unless $p(\cdot),m_0(\cdot)$ linear.

Sign flip examples: $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ equiprobable, $p(0)=p(2)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(0)=m_0(2)=0,m_0(1)=M\gg0$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0\;\forall x$, $Cov(D,X)=0$, yet $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ for $M$ large so linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta_3D+\gamma X+u$ has $\beta_3<0$ while $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. Also $m_0(x)=x^2,p(x)=x^2$ gives $\beta_3=\tau-1<0$ for $0<\tau<1$.

Sign-preserving object is non-parametric partial out $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$, i.e. $\beta_{np}=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$ and $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.

Split in room persists: 13,14,16,17,2,4,5,6,7,9,21 argue textbook saturated control reading, i.e. answer E Only Case1 and Case3, appealing to monotone $p(x),m_0(x)$ for pre-income and to $Cov(Y,D^\perp)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,8 argue literal linear OLS projection with no linearity assumptions on $E[Y|X]$ or $E[D|X]$, i.e. $Y\sim1+D+X$ is parametric linear and misspecification bias can dominate, so only Case1 is robustly sign guaranteed, answer A.

Given explicit instruction “Do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given”, the regression $Y\sim1+D+X$ is a parametric linear projection and no linearity of $m_0(\cdot)$ or $p(\cdot)$ is allowed. Under that strict reading the only robust sign guarantee for the population OLS $D$ coefficient is unconditional randomisation.

Current best judgment remains A. Only Case1. If “control for $X$’’ is understood as fully non-parametric saturated control, the textbook sign-preserving cases are 1 and 3, i.e. E, which remains the source of the unresolved intent disagreement.

Within-X sign is free: $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ and $Cov(Y,D|X)=Var(D|X)\tau(X)>0$.

Case 2. $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_D^2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.

$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]+Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)+...$
$E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$. 
$Cov(m_0(X),\tilde D)=Cov\big(m_0-{\rm Proj}m_0,\;p-{\rm Proj}p\big)$ is unrestricted under no linearity restriction on $m_0$ and $p$. Hence linear misspecification bias can dominate.
